Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning:
The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory

Minghao Guo Qingyue Jiao Xiujin Liu Jianhong Pang Ruimeng Yang Naihao Xu Liwei Che Haochen Xue Ziqi Wang Xinying Cai Jiaxuan Luo Jiaxin Deng Xuesong Ye Jintao Qu Wenyao Gao Jingwen Gu Chenyang Zhao Shichun Liu Guibin Zhang Zefang Liu Siyin Wang Wujiang Xu Danrui Li Zeru Shi Woongyeong Yeo Shuang Liu Wei-Chieh Huang Weizhi Zhang Tianyu Yang Kangsan Kim Yebowen Hu Bowen Wen Bowen Jiang Haohao Su Ming Yin Sheldon Yu Mian Zhang Yuyan Chen Hanrong Zhang Kai Mei Zihao Zhang Mingyu Jin Xi Zhu Hengyi Wang Tianxin Wei Linyong Nan Zhenwen Liang Zhendong Chu Ziqi Huang Yongye Su Sixun Dong Shujian Liu Kaiqu Liang Jiaojiao Han Zhaoye Fei Kun Wang Shihan Dou Zhichun Guo Xingjian Diao Zeqi Gu Heng Wang Tao Feng Cheng Qian Hamid Palangi Silei Xu Xi Yun Yi Zhu Shilong Liu Qingsong Wen Sung Ju Hwang Zuxuan Wu Yu-Gang Jiang Yiyu Shi Dimitris N. Metaxas Jiaxuan You Julian McAuley Mengdi Wang Jiawei Han Philip S. Yu Ziyi Ye
Abstract

Multimodal models and agents have emerged to enable AI systems to learn from and interact with the real world more like humans by integrating information across multiple modalities. However, enabling multimodal agents to continually acquire useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data remains a significant challenge as they move toward long-horizon tasks and lifelong settings. Addressing this challenge requires effective memory mechanisms that can maintain continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments, and refine memory-management policies through accumulated experience. We introduce a two-axis analytical framework for multimodal agent memory structured around two key questions: how multimodal information is formed and represented (Axis I, Formation and Representation), and how its management adapts with accumulated experience (Axis II, Memory Management). Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what information is retained and how it is encoded (e.g., modality-specific embeddings, textual and structured records, latent and parametric representations) to support subsequent reasoning and action. Axis II, Memory Management, distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through an evolving policy. Based on this framework, we synthesize recurring design patterns and derive principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction, maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions for the memory mechanism of multimodal agents.

1 Introduction

Large foundation models (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026; Google DeepMind, 2026), such as LLMs and MLLMs, have become the reasoning and perception backbones of AI agents that interpret goals, plan, use tools, and act through interaction with users and environments. An agent places the model within a continuing loop of observation, reasoning, and action (Xi et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026; Plaat et al., 2025; Chen, Celia, 2026), increasingly spanning multimodal digital and physical environments. As this interaction unfolds over time, later decisions often depend on information and experience accumulated beyond the immediately available context. Memory provides the persistent state that bridges these interactions, carrying relevant information from prior observations and experience into subsequent reasoning and action (Hu et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025e; Huang et al., 2026b).

Memory is therefore a core component of AI agents (Xu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025b). At the most basic level, it enables continuity by preserving task state and relevant experience beyond the current interaction, allowing agents to operate coherently over long horizons (Packer et al., 2023) and across repeated interactions. Beyond continuity, persistent memory allows agents to accumulate information over time, supporting personalization through user-specific experience (Hong et al., 2026) and maintaining consistent behavior as users, tasks, and environments evolve (Zhong et al., 2024). By retaining task outcomes, feedback (Shinn et al., 2023), failure traces (Tu et al., 2026), and successful strategies (Fan et al., 2026b), memory enables agents to refine future decisions and accumulate reusable knowledge (Li et al., 2024) and skills (Wang et al., 2024a).

The growing demand for agents that can interpret visual information (Nguyen et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2025c), process temporally structured video and speech (Lin et al., 2026d; Someki et al., 2026), reason about and navigate 3D spaces (Gu et al., 2024), and interact with graphical and physical environments (Agashe et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b) has made multimodal capabilities increasingly essential. To operate in these settings, an agent must integrate heterogeneous, high-dimensional observations, capture their temporal and spatial structure, and produce appropriate actions or multimodal outputs (Wang et al., 2024b). Unlike textual-only inputs, these multimodal observations cannot always be compactly or losslessly reduced to a single representation for later use. This shift does not merely increase the volume of experience an agent may encounter; it changes the nature of what must be remembered and organized. Consequently, multimodal memory must determine both what aspects of experience should persist and how those retained memories should remain useful as new observations accumulate and the underlying world evolves.

To investigate these two requirements, we characterize multimodal agent memory through a lifecycle with two coupled stages: formation determines what experience is retained and in what representation, while management governs how the resulting memory persists, changes, is accessed, and guides later reasoning and action. These stages are tightly coupled: decisions made during formation determine what evidence can later be recovered, revised, or verified, while subsequent use and new observations may require memories to be updated, reconciled, consolidated, or forgotten. Multimodality makes both stages substantially more challenging.

The first challenge arises during formation and representation: A multimodal agent must decide what experience to retain, how to divide continuous or heterogeneous observations into memory units, and in what form those memories should persist. Unlike text-centered interactions, which can be retained in a compact textual form that is directly consumable and editable (Packer et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024; Chhikara et al., 2025) by LLMs, multimodal experience may contain perceptual, temporal, spatial, and acoustic information that is expensive to preserve exhaustively and difficult to compress without loss. A memory unit may correspond to an image (Nguyen et al., 2026b), image region (Wang et al., 2026j), video frame or clip (Song et al., 2024), audiovisual event (Lin et al., 2026d), object track (Fan et al., 2024), interface state (Wang and Chen, 2025), action–observation transition (Zhang et al., 2026d), trajectory (Xu et al., 2026), or complete episode (Zhang et al., 2025c). Each unit may be stored as source media (Yu et al., 2025c), encoded as modality-specific features (He et al., 2024) or geometric state (Gu et al., 2024), abstracted into textual (Feng et al., 2026) or structured records (Long et al., 2026), compressed into a latent state (Qian et al., 2024), or internalized in model parameters (Suri et al., 2026). Each choice preserves some aspects of experience while discarding or obscuring others, creating trade-offs among fidelity, efficiency, editability, source recoverability, and compatibility with downstream reasoning and action.

The second challenge arises during memory management: the memory state formed from prior experience must remain valid as new observations arrive, tasks progress, and environments change. The central question of multimodal memory management is not only how the memory system responds as its environment changes and experience accumulates, but also how to reconcile heterogeneous and partial observations into a consistent, evolving state. New evidence may extend an existing record (Long et al., 2026), correct an earlier belief (Ma et al., 2026), invalidate stale state (Lei et al., 2025), connect previously separate events (Yan et al., 2026), or provide feedback about the effectiveness of prior memory decisions (Bärmann et al., 2026). Multimodal memory management is particularly challenging because evidence is often partial and viewpoint-dependent, while the same entity or event may be represented across source media, modality-specific features, textual summaries, and structured world states (Fan et al., 2024). Effective management must reconcile new evidence across these linked representations (Feng et al., 2026), preserve connections to the supporting observations (Lin et al., 2026d), and prevent stale or conflicting state from guiding later actions (Yeo et al., 2026b). Memory systems differ in where persistent adaptation occurs. Their responses may range from reusing formed memory without persistent change (Mu et al., 2026), to updating memory content or organization under a stable policy (Mondal et al., 2026), to using feedback to improve and evolve the policy governing future memory writing (Zou et al., 2026a), maintenance (Bärmann et al., 2026), and retrieval (Fan et al., 2026b).

Motivated by these lifecycle challenges, we present a unified analytical framework for multimodal agent memory spanning images and documents, video and audiovisual streams, audio and speech, GUI interaction, and embodied or 3D environments. Our framework organizes the field along two analytically distinct but operationally coupled axes, illustrated in Figure 1. Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what experience is retained, how it is organized into memory units, and the representation ultimately supplied to downstream reasoning or action. We distinguish source- and modality-specific representations, textual and structured representations, and latent and parametric representations, while separately examining hybrid architectures that combine multiple paths and often link compact abstractions to recoverable source evidence. Axis II, Memory Management, characterizes where persistent change occurs as experience accumulates: T1 Static Memory systems reuse formed memory without persistent modification; T2 Dynamic Memory systems update the memory state through a stable management policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory systems use feedback to update the policy governing future memory writing, maintenance, or retrieval. Together, these axes capture both what multimodal evidence survives into future computation and how the memory system evolves through continued experience.

Beyond providing a unified taxonomy, this study offers three broader contributions. First, we provide comprehensive coverage of multimodal agent memory across modalities, tasks, architectures, and evaluation settings, including a corpus of 297 memory architectures and 82 benchmark records in the current version of our taxonomy. Second, by jointly analyzing memory representation and management, we identify cross-cutting patterns that are difficult to observe from either dimension alone, including the prevalence of dynamic memory updates, the widespread use of hybrid representations, and the relative scarcity of deployment-time memory-policy evolution. Third, we synthesize the limitations of current systems and derive future directions around recoverable and provenance-aware memory, temporal validity and cross-representation consistency, self-improving memory management, bounded lifelong memory, governed forgetting, and lifecycle-aware evaluation.

This study focuses on memory mechanisms in multimodal agents. We define memory as experience-derived state that persists beyond the step in which it is formed and later affects reasoning, generation, planning, or action. At least one non-text modality must contribute to its formation or use; transient activations, one-pass reasoning traces, and incidental prompt context are excluded unless explicitly persisted and reused. Existing studies of agent memory classify memory by source (Zhang et al., 2025e), representation (Hu et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025e; Du et al., 2025), function (Hu et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2025c; Du et al., 2025), temporal scope (Wu et al., 2025c; Du et al., 2025), and operation (Zhang et al., 2025e; Du et al., 2025), while others trace its evolution from storage to reusable experience (Hu et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2026b; Luo et al., 2026a). Multimodal extensions cover LLM or MLLM memory types (Jia et al., 2025), VLM taxonomies (Xia et al., 2026a), and multimodal-agent architectures and storage (Xie et al., 2025; Mokaria et al., 2026), benchmarks (Xie et al., 2025), and applications (Xie et al., 2025; Mokaria et al., 2026). In contrast, we shift the unit of analysis from memory components to the operational lifecycle: how multimodal experience becomes persistent memory, how representation constrains subsequent retrieval, revision, and verification, and where adaptation occurs as experience accumulates.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the background, formal scope, and multimodal memory lifecycle. Section 3 studies memory formation and representation, from source-preserving and modality-native memory to explicit textual and structured representations, latent and parametric memory, and hybrid source-linked designs. Section 4 examines memory management across T1 Static Memory, T2 Dynamic Memory, and T3 Self-Evolving Memory. Section 5 analyzes how representation choices constrain memory management and synthesizes corpus-level patterns across the two axes. Section 6 examines the systems mechanisms that realize these logical memory designs under resource and coordination constraints. Section 7 examines evaluation benchmarks and applications, while Section 8 discusses open challenges and future directions. Section 9 concludes the paper.

2 Background

Multimodal agents extend foundation vision-language models from one-shot prediction to an interaction loop in which the system observes an environment, reasons about a goal, selects an action, and interprets the resulting state (Xie et al., 2025; Mokaria et al., 2026). Their observations may include text, images (Deng et al., 2026), video (Rege et al., 2026), audio (Jiang et al., 2026b), graphical interfaces (Choi et al., 2026), robot poses (Yan et al., 2025b), or other sensor streams (Lin et al., 2026c). Because these inputs accumulate across steps and often describe a changing world, the current context alone is rarely sufficient for long-horizon reasoning. Memory provides continuity by retaining selected information from earlier interaction and making it available to later decisions. Figures 2 and 3 summarize representative multimodal agent memory methods across modalities, publication years, memory-management tiers, and their growth over time.

This definition includes external evidence stores (Sun et al., 2026c), image and video banks (Fan et al., 2024), maps (Li et al., 2026i), scene graphs (Gu et al., 2024), bounded visual buffers (Wen et al., 2026), recurrent states explicitly designed as memory (Wang et al., 2025b), experience libraries (Wang et al., 2026g), executable skills (Wang et al., 2024a), and parameters generated or adapted for subsequent reuse (Suri et al., 2026). It excludes ordinary feed-forward activations, one-pass chains of thought, and incidental prompt tokens when retained state and later reuse are not part of the paper’s memory contribution.

This distinction separates memory from context. Context is the information currently exposed to a model, whereas memory is the mechanism that determines what information can survive, how it is organized, and when it can re-enter the context or policy. A retrieved image can therefore be both a stored memory item and part of the current context, while an image seen once and immediately discarded is only an observation. The distinction is especially important in multimodal systems, where storing every perceptual input is computationally impractical and often unnecessary.

In this study, we use source material to denote the external stream, document, interaction, or environment from which an agent obtains information. For each architecture, an observation is a bounded input item made available to its memory-formation process at a particular interaction step. We use evidence in a functional sense to describe an observation or identifiable memory item that is used or made available to support, ground, verify, or revise a claim, decision, action, or memory state.

Text-based-agent research established many of the designs now reused by multimodal systems: MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) organizes working, recall, and archival memory; Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) transform observation streams into higher-level reflections; MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024) combines dialogue history, user modeling, and forgetting; Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) stores feedback as reusable linguistic lessons; and Voyager (Wang et al., 2024a) preserves executable programs that can be retrieved and composed across tasks. Together, these works show that memory may serve as a context manager, a structured knowledge store, a reflective record, or a procedural skill library.

Multimodal memory inherits these functions but introduces a more difficult representation problem. Images contain spatial detail that may not be captured by a caption (Yu et al., 2025c); video and audio unfold continuously and must be segmented over time (Zhang et al., 2025d); interface observations bind appearance to actionable screen coordinates (Choi et al., 2026); and embodied experience must be associated across viewpoints, object identities, and changing locations (Fan et al., 2025; Wen and Bekris, 2021; Wen et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2026a). As a result, the decision to retain a frame (Yu et al., 2025a), caption an event (Wang et al., 2025a), fuse a 3D map (Zhu et al., 2026a), cache visual tokens (Song et al., 2026), or internalize experience in parameters (Liu et al., 2025a) changes what the agent can later recover.

Two broad strategies have emerged. Some systems preserve modality-specific evidence or states so that later computation can return to visual (Shlapentokh-Rothman et al., 2026), auditory (Someki et al., 2026), or geometric information (Liu et al., 2025b). Others translate experience into language (Feng et al., 2026), structured symbols (Long et al., 2026), shared latent spaces (Yu et al., 2026b), or parameters (Suri et al., 2026) that are easier to search and reuse. Native preservation keeps a wider range of perceptual detail but increases storage and retrieval cost. Translation produces compact and editable memory units but can remove information that was not anticipated when the memory was constructed. This trade-off motivates our memory formation and representation axis.

2.1 Classical Memory in AI & Cognitive Science

Memory has long been viewed as a requirement for intelligent behavior. In cognitive science, models often distinguish between short-lived perceptual storage, limited-capacity working memory (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974), and more durable long-term memory (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968). This view suggests that memory is not only a place to keep information, but also a mechanism for selecting, organizing, and using information during reasoning and action.

Cognitive theories also distinguish memory by function. Episodic memory stores experiences tied to particular events, while semantic memory stores general knowledge that can be reused across contexts (Tulving, 1972). Procedural memory supports skills and action routines (Squire, 1992). These distinctions are useful for agent systems because memory may preserve specific past experience (Li et al., 2026g), provide reusable abstractions (Li et al., 2026c), or support future behavior (Qin et al., 2026).

Classical AI studied memory from a computational perspective. Symbolic systems represented knowledge as facts, rules, frames, scripts, or production rules, while cognitive architectures such as SOAR (Newell, 1990) and ACT-R (Anderson et al., 2004) placed memory inside a control loop for problem solving and decision making. Case-based reasoning made experience reuse explicit by solving new problems through the retrieval and adaptation of past cases (Aamodt and Plaza, 1994). These ideas anticipate many concerns in modern agent memory, including indexing (Zhu et al., 2026c), retrieval (Qiu et al., 2026), consolidation (Chen et al., 2026c), forgetting (Mi et al., 2026), and reuse (He et al., 2026).

Neural models changed the implementation of memory. Recurrent networks store information in hidden states (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), while attention-based models can use the context as temporary memory (Vaswani et al., 2017). Memory-augmented neural networks further introduce external modules that can be read and written during computation (Graves et al., 2014; Weston et al., 2015). For modern agents, the central issue is therefore not only how information is represented internally, but also what experience persists beyond the current computation and how that retained information is later accessed or changed. This perspective connects classical memory research to the two functional stages considered in this study: formation and representation, which determine what experience is retained and in what form it reaches downstream computation, and memory management, which determines how retained memory is accessed, maintained, and adapted over time.

2.2 Foundations of Modern Agentic Memory

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides an important conceptual foundation for modern agentic memory by separating model parameters from an external, queryable information source (Lewis et al., 2020). At inference time, retrieved evidence is introduced into the model context, enabling access to information beyond parametric knowledge and the current input. In its standard form, however, RAG primarily addresses how stored information is accessed. It does not by itself specify how an agent should form memory from its own experience, maintain that memory over time, or revise it through later interactions.

Modern agent memory broadens this retrieval-centered view by treating prior interaction and experience as persistent state that can be retained, transformed, and reused across tasks or sessions. Systems such as MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023), and MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024) helped establish this shift from external knowledge retrieval toward persistent experience management. Taken together, these systems move memory beyond factual retrieval toward persistence, transformation, and experience reuse across interactions. They provide conceptual foundations for multimodal agent memory, where the same problems arise over richer forms of experience and a broader range of representations.

When considering how long-horizon agents retain and use information accumulated over extended interactions, it is important to distinguish three closely related concepts: long-context processing, context management, and memory. Long-context processing refers to a model’s capacity to capture and use information distributed across extended input sequences at manageable computational cost. Context management determines which information is included in the active context at each inference step and how it is presented to the model. Memory, as defined in this study, denotes experience-derived state that persists beyond the current inference step and subsequently influences reasoning, generation, planning, or action. Depending on its representation and integration, memory can support long-context processing by carrying historical information across input segments and support context management by selecting relevant memory content as context for the model. Long-context processing and memory augmentation serve complementary aspects for building long-horizon and lifelong agents: memory extends access to information beyond the active context, while long-context models integrate retained information from memory into current computation (Wu et al., 2022; He et al., 2025b). Beyond these functions, persistent memory enables agents to accumulate experience across interactions, tasks, and sessions, providing a substrate for inference-time adaptation and longer-term agent evolution.

2.3 The Multimodal Memory Lifecycle

Multimodal agent memory can be understood through two coupled functional stages: (1) formation and representation and (2) memory management. Formation determines what experience is retained, how it is organized, and the representation through which it becomes available to downstream computation. Memory management determines how the resulting state persists, changes, is accessed, and is used during deployment. These stages form a lifecycle rather than independent modules: management is constrained by what formation preserves, while the outcomes of memory use may trigger further formation, revision, consolidation, or forgetting. Figure 4 illustrates the two coupled stages of multimodal agent memory and the three memory-management tiers through a household-robot example.

Formation and Representation.

The first stage, formation and representation, determines what experience is saved as memory, how it is organized into memory units, and how those units are represented. The definition of a memory unit varies across modalities and levels of granularity. For static images, a unit can be an entire image, region, object, or scene (Nguyen et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026j). For video and audio, it may correspond to a keyframe, clip, event, object track, or temporally aligned audiovisual segment (Song et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2026d). In embodied settings, memory units may further capture multimodal observations, estimated world and object states, action-observation transitions, trajectories, or complete interaction (Liu et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026d; Weng et al., 2024). Once these units are formed, the agent may preserve raw or compressed sensory evidence (Fan et al., 2024), encode modality-native features or tokens (He et al., 2024), translate perceptual observations into textual or structured symbolic records (Feng et al., 2026), organize spatial and temporal relations as event graphs, scene graphs, or spatial maps (Gu et al., 2024), encode accumulated experience in recurrent latent states (Qian et al., 2024), or internalize it through updates to model parameters (Suri et al., 2026).

Memory Management.

The second stage governs how formed memories are retained, updated, accessed, and used during deployment. Axis II distinguishes three tiers according to whether the memory state and the policy that manages it change during use. T1: Static Memory stores and reuses fixed memory without modifying its content, organization, access indices, or metadata. T2: Dynamic Memory updates the memory state through a stable management policy, including appending new observations (Liu et al., 2025b), revising existing state (Feng et al., 2026), merging redundant entries (Song et al., 2024), consolidating repeated evidence (Li et al., 2026b), invalidating outdated information (Liu et al., 2026b), and forgetting under capacity constraints (Xiao et al., 2026b). T3: Self-Evolving Memory updates the memory state while also revising the policy that governs memory writing, maintenance, or access in response to feedback. Access includes the retrieval (Zhang et al., 2026e), routing (Sun et al., 2026b), or activation (Wang et al., 2026h) mechanisms that make relevant memory available to current computation. Utilization determines how the accessed information is incorporated into reasoning, generation, planning, action, or learning. These processes form a coupled management loop but remain distinct failure points: an agent may fail to retrieve relevant evidence, retrieve it but apply it incorrectly, or produce a correct output from model priors without using memory (Tang et al., 2026c; Rathi, 2026). Management is also constrained by formation and representation: no access mechanism can recover information that was discarded during formation or subsequently corrupted, invalidated, or forgotten.

Axis I, Formation and Representation, classifies the memory representation through which retained experience becomes available to downstream computation. Axis II, Memory Management, classifies systems by the scope of persistent deployment-time change they support in memory state and management policy. The resulting taxonomy is summarized in Figure 5.

3 Axis I: Formation and Representation

In Axis I, we examine how multimodal experience forms persistent memory and the representations that will be retrieved and used in future reasoning or action. As summarized in Figure 6, we classify by the representation ultimately supplied to the reasoner or action policy, rather than merely by the format used as retrieval index. Formation mechanisms determine the representational form in which raw experiences are encoded and retained as memory. This process creates distinct memory units and determines what information remains available for subsequent use. The same image, video, audio stream, or embodied episode may be retained as source evidence (Fan et al., 2024), transformed into modality-specific visual tokens (Song et al., 2024), acoustic features (Wu et al., 2026b), temporally organized video features (He et al., 2024), or geometric state (Gu et al., 2024), abstracted into linguistic (Yin et al., 2026), symbolic (Jiang et al., 2026a), relational (Long et al., 2026), or executable records (Wang et al., 2024a), or maintained as persistent latent state (Qian et al., 2024) or knowledge encoded in model parameters (Suri et al., 2026). Accordingly, we organize this axis into three families.

Many systems combine multiple representations (Yan et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026g; Huang et al., 2026c). For example, a system might use a semantic graph to locate compressed visual features and then reopen the source image for verification (Fan et al., 2024; Long et al., 2026). We therefore discuss hybrid and evidence-linked architectures separately as system-level compositions rather than as a fourth representation type.

3.1 Source- and Modality-Specific Representations

At the least abstract end of the representation axis, multimodal experiences are saved in their originating modality. We distinguish two forms. Retained source evidence preserves images (Zhang et al., 2026a), video or audio segments (Liu et al., 2026j), and sensor observations (Dorbala and Manocha, 2026) as media that the agent can reopen during inference. Modality-native encodings instead retain learned features (Diko et al., 2025), tokens (Zhao et al., 2025a), or geometric state (Honerkamp et al., 2024) that preserve modality-specific structure without requiring the original media to be processed again. Both avoid reducing experience to language or symbolic records, but they serve different priorities: source evidence remains directly verifiable and interpretable, whereas encoded state is more compact and computationally efficient but is often lossy and difficult to interpret.

3.1.1 Retained Perceptual Source Evidence

Depending on the input, these items may be complete images (Nguyen et al., 2026b), regions or crops (Choi et al., 2026), document screenshots (Yu et al., 2025c), sampled video frames (Zhang et al., 2025d), audiovisual segments (Lin et al., 2026d), RGB-D observations (Yang et al., 2025b), or observations paired with timestamps and agent poses (Yan et al., 2025b).

For static images and graphical user interfaces (GUIs), retaining visual evidence preserves layout, typography, color, fine-grained appearance, and spatial organization that textualization may discard (Yu et al., 2025c; Wang et al., 2026j). PixelRAG (Wang et al., 2026j), for example, renders webpages as screenshot tiles, indexes them using visual embeddings, and supplies the highest-ranked tiles directly to a VLM as pixel inputs. In this case, the embeddings serve only as a retrieval index, whereas the retrieved screenshots constitute the source-level visual evidence made available during inference. Source-evidence memory can also operate at different granularities: related systems retain complete screenshots (Liu et al., 2025d), action-relevant GUI regions (Choi et al., 2026), cropped interface elements (Zeng et al., 2026) , or complete visual interaction histories with frame- and region-level access (Han et al., 2026), and selectively retrieve the visual observations most relevant to the current decision.

Video and audio pose an additional access challenge because relevant evidence must first be localized within a continuous temporal stream. Existing systems address this challenge through different organizational structures (Lian et al., 2026). ToolMerge (Shlapentokh-Rothman et al., 2026) retains sampled video frames and uses an LLM planner to compose complementary visual retrieval tools, including global image-text matching, region-level entity matching, and OCR. HippoMM (Lin et al., 2026d) adopts an event-centered organization, where audiovisual experience is segmented into event records with semantic summaries, temporal boundaries, and pointers to source spans. M3-Agent (Long et al., 2026) instead organizes memory around persistent entities, linking text, image, and audio evidence to people, objects, and events over time. These designs correspond to frame-, event-, and entity-level organization, respectively, showing that retaining source media is only one part of the problem; the evidence must also be indexed at a granularity suited to later retrieval.

Spatial indexing plays a similar role in embodied agents (Li et al., 2026e). GraphEQA (Saxena et al., 2025) combines a hierarchical 3D scene graph with a task-relevant memory of images captured during exploration, allowing retrieved images to restore local visual details that may be abstracted away in the global graph. DovSG (Yan et al., 2025b) associates RGB-D observations and camera poses with a dynamic object-level map so that historical observations can support relocalization and local map refinement when the environment changes. These systems show that source evidence and structured spatial memory serve complementary roles: the structured representation supports compact, global reasoning, while linked observations preserve detailed perceptual evidence for inspection, grounding, and update.

The primary advantage of preserving source-modality evidence is recoverability: information retained in the original observation can be retrieved at different levels of granularity for later uses that may not have been anticipated during memory formation. This preserves fine-grained visual details, temporal structure (Zuo et al., 2025), acoustic cues (Someki et al., 2026), and observational context (Anwar et al., 2025), while also allowing later reasoning and actions to be grounded in and checked against specific observations.

3.1.2 Modality-Specific Encodings and Geometric State

Retaining source observations maximizes recoverability, but storing, retrieving, and repeatedly encoding every image, video frame, audio segment, or sensor observation can be prohibitively expensive for long-running agents. A more compact strategy is to persist encoded features or geometric state. We assign a memory architecture to this category when the stored value is itself consumed by the reasoner or action policy and preserves task-relevant structure inherited from the originating modality, such as spatial organization, temporal order, acoustic dynamics, or metric geometry.

Video provides the clearest setting for modality-specific encoded memory because long streams require compact representations that preserve both spatial and temporal information. Representative systems differ mainly in the granularity and consolidation strategy of the retained features. MovieChat (Song et al., 2024) accumulates frame-level visual tokens in a fixed-capacity short-term memory and repeatedly merges similar representations from temporally adjacent frames before transferring the consolidated features to long-term memory. MA-LMM (He et al., 2024) instead stores patch-level features in a visual memory bank, where they directly serve as keys and values for cross-attention; when capacity is exceeded, temporally adjacent features are merged at corresponding spatial locations. Flash-VStream (Zhang et al., 2025b) uses a coarse-to-fine design in which low-resolution feature centroids provide broad temporal coverage and high-resolution feature maps preserve detail for representative key frames. At query time, these features are combined according to their temporal positions and supplied to the language model through the visual projector. These systems illustrate three forms of encoded video memory: temporally consolidated frame tokens, spatially aligned patch features, and coarse-to-fine representations of a continuing stream. Despite their different structures, all persist visual features as the memory records itself rather than merely as retrieval indices for source frames. Modality-specific encoding can therefore limit memory growth while retaining spatial and temporal structure needed for later inference, although the resulting memory remains tied to a compatible model interface.

Image memory follows a different pattern. Representative agent systems more commonly retain decodable source images or pointers to them and use visual embeddings only for indexing and retrieval (Nguyen et al., 2026a; Deng et al., 2026). M3-Agent (Long et al., 2026), for example, stores image content alongside embeddings used for similarity-based retrieval, while M2A (Feng et al., 2026) associates stored images with textual captions and cross-modal embeddings that support both text- and image-based search. Other systems transform visual observations into textual (Gao et al., 2025) or structured records (Wen et al., 2024) and discard the source images. UniversalRAG (Yeo et al., 2026a) extends this indexing pattern across heterogeneous corpora by routing queries to modality- and granularity-specific retrievers. MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025) follows this approach for screenshot-based memory. These designs show that image encoders frequently support memory formation and retrieval, but their feature vectors less commonly serve as persistent memory values consumed directly by the downstream model.

Persistent encoded audio memory remains underexplored among the analyzed systems. Unlike speaker embeddings used only as retrieval keys (Yao et al., 2025b), such memory would preserve acoustic information as the stored value and expose it directly to the downstream model. OMAC (Wu et al., 2026b), introduced in O-MARC, provides a relevant encoding mechanism. It retains high-importance audio tokens as anchors and merges nearby discarded tokens into them through weighted aggregation. The resulting tokens remain temporally ordered and are consumed directly by a compatible omnimodal backbone without reconstructing the original waveform. OMAC therefore illustrates how acoustic features could serve as memory unit values rather than retrieval indices. However, it compresses the current audiovisual context rather than preserving information across interactions, so it is better viewed as a transferable representation mechanism than as an established example of persistent agent memory. This distinction also highlights how little persistent audio-feature memory has been explored relative to its visual counterpart.

Embodied agents extend modality-specific memory from neural feature sequences to world-centered geometric state (Huang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026a). DynaMem (Liu et al., 2025b) converts posed RGB-D observations into an evolving sparse voxel map in a global coordinate frame. Its voxels combine metric location, observation history, timestamps, and vision-language features, while new depth observations update or remove inconsistent state. This structure preserves metric relations and occupancy changes that would be difficult to recover from an unordered feature collection. A different design is to retain perceptual history for action generation rather than to construct an explicit world model. MemoryVLA (Shi et al., 2026a) compresses visual-encoder outputs into perceptual tokens that query a temporally indexed long-term bank. Retrieved history is fused with the current perceptual state and used to condition the action policy, while capacity is controlled by merging similar temporally adjacent entries. The resulting bank therefore stores a bounded history of policy-relevant visual features without reconstructing source observations. The key distinction lies in the role of memory: DynaMem organizes memory around persistent world geometry, whereas MemoryVLA organizes it around perceptual history required by the control policy.

Across these systems, the representation is decided by the structure required by the downstream interface. Video memories preserve spatial and temporal organization (He et al., 2024), emerging acoustic encodings retain temporally localized sound information (Wu et al., 2026b), geometric maps expose metric layout and occupancy (Liu et al., 2025b), and policy-facing memories retain action-relevant perceptual history (Shi et al., 2026a). Persisting these representations reduces storage, context, and repeated encoding costs while preserving information that may be difficult to express through language or symbolic records. The resulting compression is generally non-invertible: information removed through sampling (Yu et al., 2025b), merging (Song et al., 2026), clustering (Zhang et al., 2025b), spatial reduction (Guo et al., 2026a), or voxelization (Lin et al., 2026c) cannot be recovered from the encoded state alone. Learned feature memories are also model-specific and normally require a compatible projector, Q-Former, attention module, or policy interface. Geometric state is more explicitly structured, but discretization and feature aggregation can still remove perceptual detail. Modality-specific encodings and geometric state therefore trade recoverability and portability for compact, task-aligned access to perceptual and spatial structure.

3.2 Cross-Represented Explicit Memory

Multimodal experience can also be transformed into natural language or structured representations such as knowledge graphs. For example, an image may be stored as a caption (Feng et al., 2026), while an embodied observation may be represented as a scene graph containing nodes and relations between them (Gu et al., 2024). Because the relevant content is expressed through readable text or named graph components, it can be directly retrieved and used for reasoning or action. Compared with modality-specific encodings and latent or parametric memory, these representations can usually be inspected, searched, edited, or invalidated at the level of individual entries. However, their construction is also lossy: detailed visual information omitted during captioning, entity extraction, or relation construction usually cannot be recovered from the resulting representation alone.

Within Cross-Represented Explicit Memory, Perception-to-Text Records and Summaries translate multimodal experience into natural-language entries that are retrieved and supplied to the agent as text. Although these entries may be indexed by timestamps, identifiers, or embedding similarity, the content placed in the backbone LLM’s context remains textual. Spatial, Temporal, and Cross-Modal Structured Memory organizes information as graph-linked entities and relations or schema-defined fields that can be queried and updated individually. For example, a vector database of captions is textual memory, whereas a scene graph is structured memory when its nodes, relations, or topology support retrieval, reasoning, or action. Because a single architecture may combine multiple representation forms, we discuss each form in its respective section rather than assigning the architecture as a whole to a single category.

3.2.1 Perception-to-Text Records and Summaries

Textual memory expresses past experience as descriptions (Jain et al., 2025), event records (Zhang et al., 2026c), summaries (Rasheed and Kabtoul, 2026), facts (Liu et al., 2026g), profiles (Wang and Chen, 2025), or natural-language procedures (Fan et al., 2026b). Its memory unit is a linguistic entry that can be retrieved through semantic similarity, lexical matching, temporal filtering, or structured querying and then inserted directly into an LLM context. This representation aligns naturally with language-model reasoning and permits human inspection and correction without requiring a decoder. Textual memory is also well suited to evolving state because updates, corrections, and overrides can be directly incorporated into compact, ordered records, whereas modifying or reconciling multimodal evidence and its embeddings is less straightforward . It also separates storage from the original perception model: a textual memory produced by one visual or audio encoder can generally be read by another language model.

Long video provides a clear setting for this strategy because retaining every frame is expensive, while many downstream questions concern events, actions, and state changes that can be summarized linguistically. VideoAgent (Fan et al., 2024) constructs a compact semantic memory of temporal event descriptions and allows an LLM agent to query these records while deciding when additional visual evidence is needed. Video-EM (Wang et al., 2025a) makes the event abstraction more explicit. It localizes potentially relevant moments, groups them into temporally coherent events, and writes grounded episodic records containing temporal indices and when, where, what, and who cues. A chain-of-thought retrieval process then selects a minimal set of event memories for answering the current question. ReMA (Chen et al., 2026a) processes a lifelong video stream as fixed-duration clips, writes timestamp-aligned descriptions into a vector-indexed memory bank, and merges temporally overlapping observations into updated summaries. Its controller later searches these textual records and adds the results of query-directed inspections back into the same belief state. Across these systems, linguistic abstraction changes the basic memory unit from a frame to a semantically delimited event or observation, allowing temporally distant evidence to be addressed without repeatedly processing the complete video.

Textual memory is also prominent in GUI agents, where screenshots and interactions can be converted into persistent facts (Gao et al., 2025), events (Liu et al., 2025d), and workflows (Mi et al., 2026). MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025) filters visually redundant screenshots and routes new screen and conversational evidence to specialized memory managers. These managers construct natural-language summaries, event details, semantic records, workflow steps, document excerpts, and user-profile facts across six memory components. During retrieval, the system searches these components using embedding-, BM25-, or string-based methods, and the selected entries are ultimately supplied to the chat agent as labeled text. The resulting representation abstracts transient interface appearance into concepts that remain useful across later interactions, such as user activities, previously accessed resources, or recurring workflows.

Persistent image memory is less commonly represented solely in text. A single image is comparatively inexpensive to retain, while future queries may depend on typography, color, layout, object appearance, or fine spatial relations that cannot always be anticipated when a caption is written. Purely textual image memory is therefore most useful when images occur as part of a longer personal or interaction history, such as a screenshot stream or camera roll (Wang and Chen, 2025; Nguyen et al., 2026a), and the relevant memory objects are people, activities, events, or preferences rather than arbitrary visual details. In such settings, captions and event summaries provide efficient semantic access, while source images can be retained separately when later visual verification is required (Jiang et al., 2025b). This pattern explains why text-only image memory is less dominant than textual event memory for long video and interaction histories.

Pure textual memory is less common for embodied experience as well. Text can summarize observed events and completed tasks, but embodied action often depends on precise and current information about object locations, metric distances, containment, connectivity, and other spatial relations that cannot be reliably reconstructed from isolated free-form text records. Embodied systems therefore typically associate linguistic descriptions with spatial maps or entity-centered state rather than relying on unstructured text alone (Riva et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2025). Textual records remain valuable for episodic histories, task outcomes, and high-level instructions, while localization and planning generally rely on the structured representations discussed in the next section.

Across modalities, textualization provides a compact and interpretable interface between perception and reasoning. It supports semantic retrieval, direct insertion into model context, human editing, and consolidation of observations across modalities. Its primary limitation is the semantic bottleneck introduced when memories are written. Captions and summaries retain information judged salient by the formation model, but may omit visual details, flatten temporal or spatial relationships, discard acoustic cues, or introduce unsupported interpretations. Because retrieval cannot recover information that was never encoded in the textual record, the quality of textual memory depends not only on retrieval accuracy but also on the coverage, grounding, and factual reliability of the textualization process.

3.2.2 Spatial, Temporal, and Cross-Modal Structured Memory

Graphs and structured records represent experience through explicitly organized and addressable entities (Zhang et al., 2025c), attributes (Sun et al., 2026e), relations (Jiang et al., 2025a), state variables (Wang et al., 2025c), temporal links (Chang and Ren, 2026), or spatial structures (Honerkamp et al., 2024). Their meaning derives not only from the content of individual nodes or records but also from the relationships and organization among them. Accordingly, access may involve field-level lookup, graph traversal, temporal filtering, relational propagation, or spatial queries, rather than treating each entry as an independent text passage. Such representations are particularly valuable when an agent must determine not only what occurred, but also how entities are related, which state is currently valid, or where an action should be executed.

Embodied agents provide particularly clear examples of structured memory, as navigation and manipulation often require persistent representations of objects, their spatial and functional relationships, and, in dynamic environments, changes in scene state over time. ConceptGraphs (Gu et al., 2024) lifts open-vocabulary detections from successive RGB-D observations into a 3D coordinate frame and incrementally fuses them into object nodes and relational edges. The resulting scene graph supports language-grounded, object-centric, and spatial access, allowing an agent to retrieve entities and their locations for downstream perception and planning. DovSG (Yan et al., 2025b) extends this design to changing environments. It maintains persistent 3D object nodes with geometric and semantic features, connects them through spatial relations, and locally refines regions affected by robot interactions or environmental changes. The task planner reads target coordinates, object features, and graph relations to decompose instructions and support navigation, grasping, and placement. In this case, the graph is not merely an index over observations; it is the current world state on which planning operates. GraphEQA (Saxena et al., 2025) demonstrates how structured spatial memory can guide active information acquisition. During exploration, it incrementally constructs a hierarchical 3D metric-semantic scene graph containing object, room, and frontier information. The graph exposes what has already been observed, how the explored space is organized, and where additional evidence may be obtained. This state is supplied to a VLM planner that decides whether the available memory is sufficient to answer the question or whether the agent should continue exploring. Structured spatial memory therefore supports both retrospective access and prospective action: it preserves previously acquired observations while guiding the agent toward locations where additional evidence can be gathered.

Video agents impose similar structure on temporal experience. PyraVid (Yan et al., 2026) organizes streaming video into a three-level graph comprising fine-grained fact nodes, clip-level summaries, and a global narrative. Hierarchical aggregation edges connect facts to clips and clips to the global memory, while additional logical links connect related evidence across time. Retrieval begins from query-relevant seed nodes, checks whether the evidence is sufficient, and traverses the graph to expand or prune the active evidence set. WorldMM (Yeo et al., 2026b) constructs multiple temporal knowledge graphs from video segments at different resolutions and an evolving semantic graph from consolidated entity-action-entity triplets. Episodic access uses graph-based Personalized PageRank followed by cross-scale reranking, while semantic access performs edge-focused traversal over the consolidated graph. New triplets can update or remove outdated and conflicting relations. These systems show how explicit temporal and relational structure can preserve event dependencies that would be difficult to recover from an unordered collection of captions.

For persistent image memory, structured representations are particularly useful when an agent must track entities and their attributes across multiple observations. TAME (Hong et al., 2026), for example, maintains a Dynamic State Memory for transient or changing attributes and a Static Personalized Memory for stable attributes, both indexed by personalized concept identifiers. Attributes that remain stable can migrate from dynamic to static memory, while outdated attributes are removed from the bounded dynamic store. During retrieval, the system identifies the personalized concept in the current image and retrieves its associated attributes from both memories. Separating dynamic from stable attributes helps the agent distinguish transient observations, such as a recent appearance or condition, from persistent user-specific properties.

Structured visual memory can also encode the presence status of remembered concepts. PolarMem (Chen et al., 2026h) constructs a polarized graph that links visual memories to concept nodes through HAS and NOT_HAS edges, thereby distinguishing verified presence from verified absence. At query time, its logic-aware retrieval procedure enforces logical consistency before ranking candidates by semantic similarity. Memories that conflict with the query constraints are therefore suppressed even when they are semantically similar. PolarMem thus demonstrates that graph structure can represent not only associations among memory items but also positive and negative evidence. This capability is particularly valuable when an agent must explicitly rule out concepts that are visually plausible but absent from the observed evidence.

Persistent structured memory is also relatively uncommon in GUI agents. Although a GUI presents structured elements at any given moment, its layout and element hierarchy may change across application versions, window sizes, navigation states, and dynamically generated content. Memories tied to absolute screen coordinates or specific interface graphs may therefore generalize poorly across tasks and sessions. Most GUI agents more commonly retain textual interaction histories (Agashe et al., 2025) or parameterized workflow templates (Xiao et al., 2026a) that abstract away from a particular interface configuration. When structured GUI memory is used, it therefore tends to represent task state (Wang et al., 2024c), interface entities (Yu et al., 2026a), or reusable procedures (Lee et al., 2024) rather than a persistent geometric map of the interface.

Graphs and structured records support compositional queries, localized updates, temporal reasoning, and relation-aware planning that are difficult to perform over independent, free-form text. These capabilities, however, introduce substantial construction and maintenance costs. Entities must be detected and resolved across observations; attributes and relations must be extracted accurately; schemas must accommodate previously unseen concepts; and updates must maintain consistency as the environment evolves. Errors in entity creation, relation extraction, or cross-observation data association may propagate through retrieval, graph traversal, and downstream planning. Structured representations therefore improve addressability and control but do not inherently guarantee faithful memory content. Their reliability depends on both accurately transforming perceptual evidence into structured semantic content and correctly reconciling new evidence with the existing graph by updating existing entities and relations or introducing new ones.

3.3 Internalized Latent and Parametric Memory

While external memory preserves information as independently stored and retrievable artifacts, such as raw observations, textual records, structured entries, or modality-specific features, latent and parametric memory integrate experience more directly into the model’s computation. Latent memory maintains experience as continuous states that are carried and updated during inference, whereas parametric memory internalizes experience in model weights or dynamically generated adapters that shape subsequent reasoning and action.

We distinguish two forms of memory that integrate experience directly into model computation. Persistent multimodal latent states represent experience as continuous vectors, memory tokens, hidden states, or key–value units that are separate from backbone parameters. These states can be updated during inference and integrated into the model through attention, residual connections, or learned projection and fusion modules. Recent systems apply this approach to retain visual information and intermediate reasoning states (Yu et al., 2026c), coordinate memory across visual agents (Yu et al., 2026b), and compress GUI interaction histories into model-compatible continuous context (Zhang et al., 2026b). On the other hand, parametric internalization encodes experience in model weights or experience-specific adapters. Internalized memory influences subsequent inference implicitly, without requiring retrieval or inclusion of the original multimodal evidence in the input context. For example, Frames2LoRA (Suri et al., 2026) generates a LoRA adapter from a video, enabling the adapted model to use information from that video without processing its visual tokens again. Instead, MemVerse (Liu et al., 2025a) periodically distills selected knowledge from an explicit long-term memory store into a parametric memory model.

Both forms provide compact access to past experience and integrate memory closely with the model’s reasoning and control processes. They can reduce repeated encoding, retrieval costs, and context growth while retaining information that may be difficult to capture in language or symbolic structures. This close integration, however, limits direct control over the stored information. Latent and parametric memories are generally more difficult to inspect, edit, trace to specific observations, or transfer across models with incompatible architectures. Latent compression may discard information that cannot be recovered, while repeated parameter updates may cause interference or forgetting.

3.3.1 Persistent Multimodal Latent State

Common implementations use hidden states (Qian et al., 2024), memory tokens (Wang et al., 2025b), or key–value caches (Xiao et al., 2026b) and integrate them with the current input through attention, residual connections, or learned projection and fusion layers.

KV caches can also serve as persistent latent memory when they are deliberately retained and reused beyond the computation that produced them. ReKV, for example, incrementally constructs and retains video-derived KV states and selectively restores query-relevant blocks for later question answering (Di et al., 2025). MuKV further compresses multi-grained KV states to support long-horizon streaming video question answering under bounded memory (Xiao et al., 2026b).

Shared and recurrent latent states have been widely explored in image-based agents to preserve visual information and intermediate reasoning across inference steps. VisMem (Yu et al., 2026c) uses a short-term memory former to generate latent tokens containing fine-grained evidence from the current visual input, and a long-term memory former provides higher-level semantic knowledge relevant to the current reasoning context. The model learns when to invoke each memory type and inserts the resulting latent tokens into the inference sequence. TRAM (Liu et al., 2026h) preserves information from earlier reasoning steps so that it can inform later stages of a multi-step reasoning process. After each reasoning step, the model summarizes its internal activations and uses them to update two recurrent latent states with different decay rates. The fast state emphasizes recently completed reasoning, while the slow state retains information over a longer portion of the trajectory. Their combined representation is then added to selected decoder layers at the beginning of the next reasoning step. These methods address a common limitation of extended multimodal reasoning: visual evidence and intermediate conclusions may lose influence as the generation grows longer (Wu et al., 2026a).

For long video streams, latent memory can reduce the cost of repeatedly processing accumulated visual context (Chen et al., 2026c). Light-Omni (Nie et al., 2026b) maintains a bounded, non-parametric global state by progressively summarizing and merging episodic scripts. This hierarchical state preserves recent events in greater detail while representing older events through higher-level summaries. Given the global state and the current multimodal input, the model generates latent features that determine whether to speak or search and produce an embedding for retrieving relevant entries from long-term memory. Light-Omni therefore adopts a hybrid design: explicit episodic scripts and their consolidated global state preserve historical information, while the generated latent features support immediate action control and context-aware retrieval. This design is well suited to long-video tasks, which require both a compact representation of global context and access to specific events, temporal details, or original multimodal evidence.

Beyond modality-specific designs for images and video, latent memory can also support information sharing among multiple vision-language agents. L2-VMAS (Yu et al., 2026b) maintains two shared memory banks: a perception memory that stores latent representations of visual inputs and a thinking memory that stores hidden states from previous agents’ reasoning. Both are organized as key-value memory units that can be retrieved and integrated into subsequent agent computation.

GUI agents use latent memory to connect interaction history with the current interface state (Wu et al., 2025b). Mem-W (Zhang et al., 2026b) uses a shared trajectory-to-latent compressor to encode two sources of GUI memory: completed trajectories retrieved from an external memory bank and the expired prefix of the current interaction. The resulting memory tokens are combined with the task instruction, current screenshot, and recent observation-action context in a unified continuous embedding sequence. Retrieved trajectories provide procedural evidence from both successful and failed experiences, while the compressed in-session history preserves unfinished task progress. Both forms of experience can therefore directly inform the agent’s next action without being converted into textual summaries. This representation is well suited to GUI tasks, where the relevant state is distributed across visual observations, previous actions, and intermediate task progress.

This approach extends naturally from GUI interaction to embodied control, where agents must relate current observations to previous actions and task progress (Li et al., 2026j). LaMem-VLA (Qu et al., 2026) organizes an agent’s interaction history into two complementary memory vaults: a short-term vault that retains recent visual information and a long-term vault that preserves task progress and action continuity. Given the current observation and instruction, the model retrieves relevant information from both vaults and compresses it into fixed-length latent memory tokens. These tokens are combined with the current visual, instruction, and action-query tokens in a unified embedding sequence, allowing historical experience to directly guide action generation . This design is well suited to Vision-Language-Action (VLAs) models because it integrates perception, memory, and control within a shared continuous representation space.

Persistent latent memory remains relatively underexplored in audio and speech agents. These systems more commonly preserve semantic content as transcripts (Jiang et al., 2026b) and represent speaker identity, prosody, and other acoustic properties as separately accessible features (Someki et al., 2026). Such representations support direct retrieval and speaker attribution while retaining temporal and acoustic evidence that recurrent compression may discard. Consequently, persistent latent states designed to preserve general auditory experience across long interactions or multiple episodes remain less developed than their counterparts in visual reasoning, GUI interaction, and embodied control.

Across modalities, latent memory operates over different persistence horizons. Some latent states are maintained within a single reasoning trajectory (Yu et al., 2026c; Liu et al., 2026h), whereas others preserve information across successive agents or interaction steps (Yu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b). Latent representations may also be constructed on demand from retrieved long-term experience (Zhang et al., 2026b; Qu et al., 2026). Despite these differences, these mechanisms share a common property: past experience is represented in a continuous form that directly contributes to subsequent model computation.

3.3.2 Experience-Conditioned Parametric Memory

A system may update shared model parameters through gradient-based learning (Lin et al., 2026e) or encode experience in instance- or task-specific adapters attached to a frozen backbone (Wang et al., 2026d; Wang et al., 2026k). Once encoded in shared weights or a selected adapter, the information influences model computation without retrieving the original observations or adding them to the input context.

Image-based parametric memory has primarily been explored through multimodal knowledge editing, where the objective is to retain newly introduced or corrected visual facts within a model. MemEIC (Seong et al., 2025) adopts a hybrid design that combines explicit evidence with parametric internalization. It maintains separate LoRA adapters for visual and textual knowledge updates while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. A visual edit updates only the visual adapter, whereas a textual edit updates only the textual adapter. During inference, the system activates the adapter associated with the query modality; when a query requires both modalities, it activates both adapters and uses a learned connector to combine their representations. This design illustrates both an advantage and a challenge of parametric memory. Incorporating an edit into learned parameters allows the updated knowledge to participate directly in subsequent computation, but repeatedly writing heterogeneous information into shared parameters can cause interference and forgetting. MemEIC addresses this problem by separating parameter updates by modality, while retaining explicit edit records externally for reliable retrieval and verification.

Video introduces a different motivation for parametric memory: supporting repeated queries without retaining and reprocessing a long sequence of visual tokens. Frames2LoRA (Suri et al., 2026) first encodes a video using a frozen vision-language model. A Perceiver-based hypernetwork then converts the resulting layer-wise representations into a video-specific LoRA adapter in a single forward pass. This adapter is attached to the frozen model and acts as a reusable parametric representation of the video. For each subsequent question, the model receives only the textual query, while information from the video influences its response through the adapter parameters; neither the original video nor its visual tokens are included in the input context. Unlike conventional per-video fine-tuning, the method does not iteratively optimize a new adapter for each video. Instead, its trained hypernetwork directly generates the adapter from the video representations. Frames2LoRA therefore demonstrates how parametric memory can convert a particular video into a compact and reusable parameter component, reducing the cost of repeated inference while sacrificing direct access to the original visual evidence.

In GUI agents, parametric memory more commonly captures reusable operational knowledge than the appearance of a particular screen (Jin et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026e). SE-GA (Jin et al., 2026b) illustrates this form of experience internalization through a hybrid memory architecture. During task execution, its Test-Time Memory Extension component maintains an explicit repository containing current task state, general GUI rules, and successful trajectories from previous tasks. Its Memory-Augmented Self-Evolution pipeline subsequently uses the accumulated interaction data to improve the agent’s policy through grounding supervision and reinforcement learning, with parameter-efficient LoRA updates used during self-evolution. The explicit repository makes recent and task-specific experience immediately retrievable, whereas the learned policy parameters absorb recurring interaction patterns so that they can influence future actions without replaying every source trajectory. SE-GA therefore exemplifies a slower form of parametric consolidation in which accumulated GUI experience is converted into a more general action policy. Fully parametric, episode-specific GUI memory remains uncommon because successful interaction often depends on exact screenshots, interface states, and action histories that are easier to inspect, revise, and reuse when retained explicitly.

Embodied control provides a clear example of parametric memory stored in separate, reusable adapters. Rather than merging all experience into the model’s shared weights, VLA-Pro (Si et al., 2026) maintains task-specific LoRA adapters that can be retrieved and combined according to the current situation. VLA-Pro first trains a shared LoRA adapter across previously seen manipulation tasks and then learns a separate task-specific adapter for each task. Each memory entry pairs its adapter with a sequence of structured procedural states describing when the stored behavior is relevant. These states specify the action type, object geometry, end-effector orientation, and target interaction point. Given the current visual observation, language instruction, and interaction history, the system extracts the agent’s current procedural state and retrieves the most relevant task memories. It then combines their LoRA adapters using similarity-based weights, temporarily attaches the fused adapter to the vision-language-action model, and uses the adapted policy to generate the next action chunk. VLA-Pro demonstrates that parametric memory need not be incorporated permanently into a single set of shared weights. Parameterized experiences can instead remain modular, indexed by explicit descriptors, and selectively composed according to the current situation. This organization achieves a milestone improvement in cross-task transfer while limiting interference from unrelated manipulation behaviors.

Together, these systems show that parametric memory can operate at different granularities and persistence horizons. MemEIC (Seong et al., 2025) accumulates modality-specific knowledge edits, Frames2LoRA (Suri et al., 2026) generates a separate adapter for each video, SE-GA (Jin et al., 2026b) consolidates interaction experience into a shared GUI policy, and VLA-Pro (Si et al., 2026) stores task-specific action adapters that can be retrieved and composed. Their common property is that past information influences later computation through learned parameters rather than solely through replayed observations or records. Parametric memory can therefore reduce repeated context processing and support direct behavioral adaptation, but it also makes the underlying evidence less accessible and introduces challenges in updating, attribution, interference control, and deletion. Consequently, many multimodal agents combine parametric internalization with explicit memory that preserves source evidence and provides more controllable access.

3.4 Hybrid Representations

The preceding subsections describe three primary forms of multimodal memory: source- and modality-specific evidence, textual and structured records, and latent or parametric representations. Each form offers different advantages. Source evidence preserves perceptual detail, textual and structured records support efficient retrieval and explicit reasoning, and latent or parametric representations can contribute directly to model computation. In practice, however, no single form is sufficient for every memory operation. Hybrid memory is not an additional elementary encoding type; rather, it describes how different representations are organized and used together within a memory system. An important subtype is source-linked memory, in which an abstract record retains a reference to the original observation or to selected evidence preserved from it. The agent can then search and reason over compact abstractions while recovering the corresponding image, frame, audio segment, or interface region when finer perceptual evidence is required.

For collections of images and visually rich documents, hybrid representations allow an agent to organize large amounts of retrieved evidence without reducing all visual content to text (Wang et al., 2026a). VimRAG (Wang et al., 2026e) represents iterative multimodal retrieval and reasoning as a directed acyclic graph. Each node records its dependencies on earlier nodes, the subquery that produced it, a concise textual summary, and a multimodal memory bank containing visual tokens from retrieved images or video frames. The graph exposes the temporal and logical structure of the reasoning process, while the visual tokens preserve information that may be lost in textual summarization. To operate under a bounded context budget, VimRAG dynamically adjusts the number of visual tokens retained for each memory item according to its semantic relevance, recency, and position in the reasoning graph. The method therefore demonstrates a combined hybrid representation: structured and textual components organize the agent’s reasoning state, whereas continuous visual representations preserve perceptual information for later verification and answer generation.

Video streams create a stronger need to connect compact semantic records with recoverable visual evidence because relevant events may occur far apart, and details omitted during summarization may become important only after a query is received. FOLIO (Fan et al., 2026a) combines a short-term buffer of recent frames, a long-term semantic memory, and a visual-evidence cache. As the video arrives, the system constructs structured records describing entities, attributes, locations, relations, actions, and state changes. These records contain timestamps and references to selected keyframes retained in the evidence cache. At query time, FOLIO retrieves relevant semantic records and can restore their associated keyframes when additional visual grounding is needed. The structured memory supports efficient long-horizon access, while the linked frames preserve visual details that the records may omit or describe incorrectly. FOLIO thus exemplifies source-linked hybrid memory: semantic abstraction reduces the cost of storing and searching a long video, but it does not permanently replace the observations from which the memory was derived.

In GUI interaction, source linkage is useful because a textual description may capture the meaning of an earlier interface event while omitting the precise visual target or interface state needed for a later action. MementoGUI (Zeng et al., 2026) maintains both within-episode working memory and cross-episode episodic memory. For a selected interaction step, a working-memory entry contains a textual event summary, the bounding box of the relevant interface region, a crop of that region, and a visual embedding used only to organize the memory. When older entries are compressed, their textual content is summarized, but identifiers for selected visual regions are retained and later resolved back into the corresponding crops. Episodic-memory entries similarly combine trajectory summaries and action metadata with representative interface crops and retrieval embeddings. During action generation, the agent receives the retrieved textual summaries and region-of-interest images through the frozen GUI model’s standard multimodal input interface. MementoGUI therefore represents interface experience through source-linked textual and visual components: text records task progress and the significance of earlier events, while linked crops recover localized details such as icons, labels, selected values, and interface states. Its retrieval embeddings serve only as indices and do not themselves constitute the memory records to be retrieved and used.

In interactive visual environments, hybrid memory can combine a continuously revised semantic state with a complete record of visual interaction, since details that appear unimportant at one step may become useful later. VISTA (Han et al., 2026) maintains two forms of memory in parallel: revisable textual notes that summarize reusable environment knowledge and the agent’s current state, and a lossless visual memory that stores every returned frame in its original form.
