During reasoning, the agent can rely on the compact textual state for routine planning while selectively revisiting arbitrary past frames or spatial regions when finer-grained perceptual evidence is needed. Unlike source-linked designs in which individual abstract records explicitly reference particular observations, VISTA keeps its textual state and visual history separately addressable and combines them on demand.

Embodied agents require hybrid memory to preserve perceptual evidence while organizing it according to the spatial structure of the environment (Li et al., 2026e). ObsGraph (Lee et al., 2026) constructs an observation-centered hierarchical scene graph with room, view, and object layers. Room-level representations provide coarse semantic anchors, view-level memories preserve observations in which multiple objects appear together, and object-level memories retain fine-grained visual information about individual objects. Relations among these layers connect object evidence to the views and rooms in which it was observed. Given a task, the agent retrieves memory progressively from rooms to views and objects under a bounded budget. The level at which relevant evidence is missing also determines whether the agent should search another room, refine an existing viewpoint, or explore an unobserved frontier. ObsGraph therefore combines semantic hierarchy, spatial structure, and retained visual observations. The structured graph supports efficient retrieval and planning, while its linked visual evidence preserves appearance and co-visibility information that semantic labels alone cannot express. This combination is particularly important in embodied settings because memory must support not only retrospective question answering but also decisions about where to move and what additional evidence to acquire. Beyond navigation, HiMe (Ji et al., 2026) addresses long-horizon manipulation with a hierarchical hybrid-memory architecture that combines recent visual working memory, image–text contextual records, and a structured procedural plan to retain evolving object states and task progress across action sequences.

Across modalities, hybrid representations exploit the strengths of different memory forms. Textual and structured records provide compact semantic access, explicit relations, and controllable updates, whereas retained observations and modality-specific representations preserve perceptual detail and the provenance of abstracted information. Their combination enables a tiered access strategy: agents can rely on compact abstractions for routine retrieval and reasoning, while selectively recovering higher-fidelity evidence when a task requires verification, reinterpretation, or details lost during abstraction. This capability is likely to become increasingly important as multimodal agents operate over longer histories and in dynamic environments, where retaining all observations in the active context is impractical but irreversible compression is unreliable. Hybrid memory may therefore emerge as a prominent design pattern, particularly for applications in which both efficiency and evidential grounding are important. Its effectiveness, however, depends on more than storing multiple representations. Systems must preserve valid links as memories are revised, merged, or removed; maintain consistency between abstract records and their supporting observations; and learn when compact memory is sufficient and when source evidence should be restored. The central challenge is thus to coordinate representations of different fidelity, cost, and accessibility so that an agent can move between efficient abstraction and grounded perceptual recall as its information needs change.

4 Axis II: Memory Management

After forming memory records from raw messages, experience, and related metadata, the memory system must control how these representations are maintained, accessed, and changed as experience accumulates. Figure 7 summarizes this progression from T1 Static Memory to T2 Dynamic Memory and T3 Self-Evolving Memory. Specifically, memory management operations include writing, updating, consolidation, reorganization, retention, and forgetting, while retrieval selects relevant memory for ongoing reasoning and action. These operation mechanisms may be governed by heuristic rules (Yang et al., 2025b), fixed prompts (Ali et al., 2025), frozen learned modules (Li et al., 2026a), optimization procedures (Wang et al., 2026m), or policies that themselves adapt from deployment feedback (Zou et al., 2026a).

Multimodal memory introduces another representational challenge compared to textual inputs. Multimodal inputs are often high-dimensional and expensive to retain in their original form. Therefore, systems must balance storage and retrieval efficiency against the ability to recover source evidence, leading to the diverse representation choices discussed in Axis I. Hybrid systems may preserve multiple representations to balance information fidelity and computational efficiency. Consequently, multimodal memory management involves not only updating memory content but also maintaining consistency across these linked representations. It must determine which representations should change, how updates should propagate among related representations, and whether abstracted memories remain valid and grounded in their source evidence as experience accumulates. Conceptually, we can model these representations as nodes in a representation graph connected by transformation, alignment, fusion, and grounding relations. Memory operations then act on both the representation states and the relations connecting them. We distinguish three tiers according to what can change during inference.

The distinction between memory-state updates and policy evolution depends on the function of the updated component. Memory state includes stored content, organization, access indices, and descriptive metadata, while the management policy governs how memory operations are selected and performed. Changes to retrieval keys, skill descriptions, or usage statistics can alter subsequent retrieval results without changing this policy. Such changes should remain within T2 Dynamic Memory when the selection and update mechanisms remain stable. T3 Self-Evolving Memory goes beyond state modification by using feedback to persistently revise reusable management rules, instructions, procedures, or learned policy components.

Accordingly, the three tiers distinguish whether the memory state and the policy that manages it change during inference. Axis II, Memory Management, organizes systems by the scope of persistent deployment-time change they support. Across these tiers, multimodal information may remain within one representation, be projected into another representation, be fused across multiple modalities, or be jointly maintained across linked representations. The tiers therefore progress from reusing fixed memory, to updating memory through a stable policy, and finally to updating memory through an evolving policy, while the transition patterns characterize how multimodal information moves through the representation system. Updating memory state and evolving management policies can help agents adapt to changing environments and mitigate training–deployment mismatch, but these changes may also introduce instability and make memory updates harder to control. The following subsections examine memory access and reuse in T1 Static Memory, five memory-state operations in T2 Dynamic Memory, and the evolution of writing, maintenance, and retrieval policies in T3 Self-Evolving Memory.

4.1 T1: Static Memory

T1 Static Memory is well suited to large, static corpora (Yu et al., 2025c), stable knowledge bases (Yu et al., 2025c; Hu et al., 2023), and invariant environment or task information that must be retrieved and reused across subsequent reasoning steps or tasks, such as long-video analysis (Fan et al., 2024) or navigation with a preconstructed environment map (Huang et al., 2025). The absence of an update policy preserves the memory state across tasks and prevents unverified outputs from modifying it. Representative systems across modalities follow this pattern by constructing memory before downstream task execution and leaving it unchanged during subsequent use (Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025d; Li et al., 2026d).

Because T1 Static Memory undergoes a single formation cycle, its stored representations and their relationships remain unchanged after formation. Subsequent access and retrieval operations neither modify nor reorganize the persistent memory. Accordingly, the principal design variables in T1 Static Memory systems are the indexing and retrieval mechanisms, which may be optimized during system development or memory formation but remain fixed during inference. Fixed multimodal memories may be organized as flat sequential records (Wu et al., 2025a), vector-indexed collections (Wang et al., 2026g), hierarchical or multi-tier (Wang et al., 2026c), relational graphs (Su et al., 2026), inference-time latent states (Wu et al., 2025b), or parametric modules (Si et al., 2026). Retrieval-augmented generation provides a common access framework for vector-indexed memory, using dense cross-modal similarity, late interaction, or reranking to retrieve relevant images, document pages, video segments, audio spans, or cross-represented textual records (Yu et al., 2025c; Wang et al., 2026j; Yeo et al., 2026a; Fan et al., 2024). Metadata-aware and spatiotemporal retrieval further exploits timestamps, locations, speaker identities, and temporal boundaries to localize relevant experiences, sometimes through hierarchical coarse-to-fine search (Jiang et al., 2025b; Someki et al., 2026). Relational memories support explicit traversal over connections among objects, states, events, or interface transitions (Shen et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026a). Planner- or tool-assisted retrieval decomposes a query and routes its subqueries to modality-specific indexes, temporal search tools, or structured databases (Fan et al., 2024; Someki et al., 2026). Inference-time latent-state and parametric memory systems are less common in this setting because their stored information is less explicit and interpretable (Suri et al., 2026).

In practice, static memory supports three main types of downstream applications: static knowledge bases, reusable evidence or environment stores, and reusable procedural knowledge. First, it can retain external knowledge or documentation for domain-specific applications, such as medicine, thereby improving grounding and reducing hallucinations (Xia et al., 2025). Second, it can store expensive-to-process but largely static content, such as long videos (Fan et al., 2024) or GUI environments (Wen et al., 2024), through one-time ingestion and reuse this information across subsequent tasks (Fan et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2024). Finally, static memory can preserve procedural knowledge for repeated action planning and execution (Si et al., 2026).

T1 Static Memory is most effective when the underlying information changes slowly and the stored representation will be reused across tasks. Expensive operations such as document encoding, video analysis, environment exploration, and adapter training are performed during memory formation. Because the stored content remains unchanged, each task accesses the same evidence, environment model, or procedural library. This stability supports consistent behavior.

However, this stability limits the system’s ability to respond to change. T1 Static Memory preserves both the useful information and any omissions or errors introduced during its formation. During normal task execution, it cannot incorporate corrections to stored evidence, changes in an interface or physical environment, or procedural knowledge gained from later successes and failures. The stored representation may therefore become incomplete or outdated as the source, environment, or task distribution changes.

4.2 T2: Dynamic Memory

We organize T2 Dynamic Memory methods around five fundamental memory operations.

In multimodal memory systems, the central design challenge is to perform these operations across heterogeneous representations while preserving relevant information and cross-modal relationships. Therefore, to systematically examine T2 Dynamic Memory methods, we characterize each fundamental memory operation along two multimodal-specific dimensions. The representation-handling pattern indicates whether an operation acts locally within a single representation, coordinates distinct representations while keeping them separable, or transforms information across representations through projection or fusion. The computational mechanism specifies how the resulting memory change is produced: through hard-coded heuristics, a prompted LLM, a trained functional update module, or iterative optimization under a fixed objective.

4.2.1 Memory Update

Memory update incorporates new observations, interactions, or feedback into persistent memory. Depending on the target representation, an update may append new evidence, revise an existing record, modify a structured state, integrate information into a latent state, or edit specific model parameters. The central multimodal challenge is to incorporate new information while preserving existing content in abstract representations, cross-modal alignment, and relationships among linked representations.

Source-preserving memories incorporate new information by inserting observations, replacing outdated evidence, or modifying associated metadata. Source-preserving memories commonly incorporate new information by appending raw or minimally processed multimodal observations to an evidence log or feature buffer, thereby retaining prior perceptual evidence without rewriting it (Diko et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026). The appended evidence may include metadata, source links, or derived retrieval indices that support efficient access while preserving the original observations (Feng et al., 2026).

Modality-specific feature representations are generally updated through within-modality matching followed by feature aggregation or insertion. Each incoming feature is compared with stored representations from the same modality. If a match is identified, the corresponding memory entry is augmented, averaged, or replaced; otherwise, a new entry is created. This mechanism preserves modality-specific evidence while using shared entity identifiers to coordinate related information across modalities (Long et al., 2026).

Geometric memory representations are updated by first registering new observations within a common spatial reference frame and then associating the projected measurements or detected instances with existing spatial elements. Matched elements may be updated through feature fusion or attribute modification, whereas unmatched observations may create new map cells, objects, nodes, or relations. Invalid or obsolete elements may likewise be removed (Liu et al., 2025b; Jiang et al., 2025a; Mitash et al., 2020). These predefined association and fusion procedures provide explicit control over spatial updates and help preserve geometric consistency, but their reliability depends on fixed matching criteria and their robustness to noisy, incomplete, or conflicting observations.

Structured memory representations organize information as entities, relations, events, or procedures. New information is incorporated by identifying the relevant structural unit and then modifying its attributes, inserting or removing nodes and edges, adjusting relation weights, or updating transition statistics. Target units may be selected through similarity-based gating, while their indices and relations are maintained through moving-average aggregation, count updates, and graph-editing operators (Jiang et al., 2026a).

Textual semantic records derived from multimodal experience retain perceptual or interaction information as natural-language facts, attributes, or event descriptions. Unlike structured memories, whose updates modify explicit entities, relations, or topology, these records are maintained through content-level semantic edits. Updating them requires interpreting incoming evidence relative to existing content and selecting an operation such as addition, modification, confirmation, deletion, or no change. Prompted LLMs or VLMs are used to perform this comparison because the system must determine whether new evidence confirms, extends, contradicts, or supersedes an existing record from the multimodal experience (Feng et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Ji et al., 2026).

Latent memory incorporates new information through trained parameterized modules that either transform an existing latent state or construct new latent memory entries. Recurrent state-transition modules integrate the preceding latent state with the current multimodal representation to produce a successor state (Qian et al., 2024). Query-based write modules instead distill incoming features, instructions, and retrieved context into compact tokens that are added to a latent memory bank (Diko et al., 2025). Thus, the former modifies an existing latent representation, whereas the latter expands the memory with newly constructed latent entries. Because both forms distribute information across latent vectors, their updates are generally difficult to inspect, attribute to specific observations, or correct selectively.

Parametric memory incorporates new information by routing it to a designated subset of model parameters and optimizing those parameters under a fixed editing objective (Liu et al., 2025a). Modality-specific adapters can restrict visual and textual edits to separate parameter subsets, limiting interference across modalities and unrelated model behavior (Seong et al., 2025). Unlike a trained functional module, which computes the next memory state through a forward pass, a parametric editor produces the updated memory through inference-time optimization. The central challenge is to internalize new information while preserving previously stored knowledge and maintaining the model’s behavior on unrelated inputs.

Hybrid memory systems coordinate updates across multiple representational forms, such as source evidence, semantic records, latent tokens, and model parameters. Common mechanisms include linking editable semantic records to immutable source evidence (Feng et al., 2026), maintaining compact latent representations alongside detailed perceptual features (Diko et al., 2025), and coupling parametric edits with corresponding external records (Seong et al., 2025). These coordinated pathways preserve the complementary properties and provenance of different representations. However, they must keep linked memory components consistent as new information is incorporated, without collapsing representational distinctions or breaking associations.

4.2.2 Memory Consolidation

Memory consolidation transforms related stored information into a less redundant, more compact representation. Unlike update, which incorporates an incoming experience, consolidation operates across accumulated memories. Its central multimodal challenge is to reduce storage and retrieval costs without removing perceptual details, temporal distinctions, modality-specific evidence, or cross-representation links that may remain important for later reasoning. Existing mechanisms primarily perform feature-space compression, semantic abstraction, structured merging, or coordinated consolidation across representations (Lian et al., 2026).

Feature-space compression reduces redundancy among stored perceptual or latent encodings. Temporally adjacent or semantically similar visual features can be selected through fixed similarity criteria and then averaged (He et al., 2024), clustered (Zhang et al., 2025b), or merged (Song et al., 2026) into a smaller set of representative tokens. More adaptive mechanisms vary the degree of compression according to temporal change or semantic salience, preserving more features around distinctive events while compressing repetitive observations more aggressively (Song et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2025a). FluxMem (Xie et al., 2026b), for example, achieves competitive performance by retaining recent observations at full resolution, removing temporally redundant tokens from mid-term memory, and further consolidating spatially repetitive regions in long-term memory. These mechanisms bound memory growth, but overly aggressive compression may remove brief actions, fine visual details, or temporal transitions that cannot be recovered from the consolidated features.

Semantic abstraction can likewise consolidate a growing video history in language space. ReMA (Chen et al., 2026a) first appends timestamp-aligned descriptions for successive video clips. Whenever a new passive or query-directed observation overlaps existing temporal nodes, a prompted summarizer merges the old and new content and replaces those nodes with a unified record; non-overlapping observations are added as new entries. The same procedure operates during initial stream ingestion and recursive query answering, so the belief state continues to change while the memory-management policy remains stable. ReMA therefore exemplifies consolidation in T2 Dynamic Memory rather than policy evolution in T3 Self-Evolving Memory: task-specific inspection can refine what is stored, but task outcomes do not update the rule governing later memory operations.

Structured merging consolidates memories whose internal organization must be preserved. Graph alignment and matching procedures identify equivalent entities, actions, or procedural steps before merging their nodes, edges, alternative paths, and associated statistics (Yeo et al., 2026b). Recurring action sequences may also be extracted from multiple episodes and converted into reusable procedural structures (Jiang et al., 2026a). Unlike feature averaging, structured merging must determine which elements are genuinely equivalent and which represent meaningful alternatives; incorrect alignment can collapse distinct entities, actions, or execution paths.

Coordinated cross-representation consolidation creates a compact representation while retaining links to complementary forms of evidence. A visual sequence may be compressed into representative features and paired with a textual clue (Xiong et al., 2025), an audiovisual episode may be summarized while preserving timestamps and representative frames (Yan et al., 2026), or an entity-level fact may remain linked to the observations from which it was derived (Ma et al., 2026). This coordination allows the compact memory to support efficient retrieval while the linked source or lower-level representation preserves details omitted during abstraction. The central requirement is therefore not to preserve every representation at equal resolution, but to maintain sufficient links for the consolidated memory to be interpreted, verified, or expanded when needed.

4.2.3 Memory Revision

Memory revision corrects an existing memory when new evidence indicates that its content is inaccurate, inconsistent, incomplete, or outdated. The revision operation is narrower than update: adding an independent observation constitutes an update, whereas modifying or replacing an existing record in response to conflicting or superseding evidence constitutes revision. It also differs from forgetting, which removes information because of capacity, recency, or importance rather than because new experiences show the information to be incorrect. In multimodal systems, revision primarily involves spatial and object-state correction, semantic revision, and conflict reconciliation across linked representations.

Spatial and object-state correction revises geometric or structured environment memory when new observations indicate that an object has moved, disappeared, changed state, or been incorrectly associated with an existing entity. The mechanism registers each new observation within a common spatial reference frame and identifies the affected object or map region through geometric and semantic matching. It then replaces outdated attributes, removes invalid entities, updates object geometry, or recomputes spatial relations within the affected subgraph (Jiang et al., 2025a; Yan et al., 2025b). Restricting revision to the affected region avoids reconstructing the entire environment representation, but reliable correction requires maintaining object identity despite occlusion, viewpoint changes, and noisy observations.

Semantic revision operates on explicit facts, attributes, and event records derived from multimodal experience. Incoming evidence is compared with existing records to determine whether it confirms, extends, contradicts, or supersedes their content. Prompted LLMs or VLMs commonly perform this comparison and select among fixed operations such as modification, replacement, deletion, confirmation, or no change (Feng et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Yeo et al., 2026b). Effective revision must correct outdated information without replacing compatible records merely because the new observation is incomplete or expressed differently.

Cross-representation conflict reconciliation is required when the same experience is retained as source evidence and as one or more derived semantic or structured records. Evidence identifiers or entity associations can be used to retrieve the observations supporting a disputed record before the record is revised. The correction is then applied to the derived representation while its links to the supporting visual, auditory, or interaction evidence are retained (Feng et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026). This mechanism preserves provenance and supports later verification, but it must determine whether an apparent conflict reflects a genuine change, an unreliable observation, or information that is valid only under a different temporal or situational context.

4.2.4 Memory Reorganization

Memory reorganization changes the structural role, placement, or access path of information that remains in memory. It does not primarily add observations, correct content, or combine multiple memories. Instead, it determines where retained information resides and how it is connected or retrieved. Multimodal memory systems primarily perform reorganization through tier migration, graph relinking, and cross-representation reindexing or association.

Tier migration transfers retained memory records between storages with different temporal or functional roles, such as short- and long-term memory or dynamic and static memory. A fixed trigger first identifies information that meets a capacity, persistence, or stability criterion, then moves or copies it to the appropriate destination. Compact visual representations can be transferred from a bounded short-term buffer into long-term memory (Song et al., 2024), while attributes judged to be persistent can migrate from dynamic conversational state into static personalized memory (Hong et al., 2026). Here, tiers denote temporal or functional memory roles rather than hardware storage levels. Moving an unchanged artifact between accelerator memory, host memory, and storage is a physical residency decision, discussed in Sections 6.1 and 6.2; it does not by itself reorganize the logical memory.

Graph relinking changes the relations through which retained entities or events are structurally connected. When an embodied scene changes, links involving affected objects can be invalidated and spatial relations within the local subgraph recomputed without rebuilding the complete scene representation (Yan et al., 2025b). Relinking can also establish or reinforce associations between separately retained modality-specific evidence, such as face and voice representations that are determined to refer to the same persistent entity (Long et al., 2026). These mechanisms support entity continuity and cross-modal traversal, but incorrect associations can connect unrelated evidence or propagate a local error through the graph.

Cross-representation reindexing changes the retrieval representation associated with retained content without necessarily modifying the underlying content or the retrieval policy. Incoming observations can be compared with the goal- and step-level index vectors associated with an existing procedural graph, after which the matched vectors are adjusted through a fixed moving-average rule (Jiang et al., 2026a). The procedure itself remains unchanged, but its retrieval keys can be updated so that varied descriptions of the same task can reach a shared procedural memory. More generally, reindexing and association maintenance keep dense retrieval keys, modality-specific identifiers, and structured memory items aligned as experience accumulates (Zhu et al., 2026c; Yan et al., 2026). Excessive index drift or incorrect identity association, however, may make earlier access paths unreliable.

4.2.5 Memory Forgetting

Memory forgetting controls which accumulated information should remain available to the agent and at what level of detail. The forgetting operation may remove an item from an active store, reduce the detail preserved in one representation, or lower a memory’s priority during retrieval. In multimodal systems, forgetting need not affect every representation of an experience equally: detailed perceptual evidence may leave active memory while a compact event record, textual summary, or linked long-term representation remains available. The major mechanisms in the current literatures are active evidence eviction, representation-detail decay, semantic accessibility decay, and coordinated selective forgetting across linked representations.

Active evidence eviction removes source-preserving evidence or their encodings from a bounded active memory. Selection may follow insertion order such as first-in, first-out (FIFO), event-level reservoir sampling, object identity, frequency and recency statistics, or recency-weighted retention probabilities (Lin et al., 2026c; Wen et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025c; Xiong et al., 2025). Eviction bounds active-memory cost, and removal from the active buffer does not imply that all information derived from the observation has been erased from long-term memory. They can be reorganized or migrated to another memory store before being forgotten.

Representation-detail decay retains a memory in its source modality while progressively reducing the detail or size of its representation. Interaction histories rendered as memory images can be downsampled as they recede in time, therefore reducing their resolution and visual-token allocation while a more detailed textual record remains available (Li et al., 2026h). Optical-forgetting mechanisms similarly apply progressive resolution reduction to visually represented memory pages, preserving coarse semantic structure while discarding fine visual details (Chang and Ren, 2026).

Semantic accessibility decay preserves the content of an episodic or semantic record while lowering its retrieval priority. A time-dependent decay factor can reduce a record’s retrieval priority over time, while repeated recall or contextual relevance may restore its priority (Liu et al., 2025a). When retrieval priority decreases, the memory remains stored but becomes less likely to enter the agent’s working context. This mechanism provides more gradual control than eviction, although an overly aggressive decay function may render stored experiences effectively inaccessible.

Coordinated selective forgetting operates on experiences stored in multiple representations and determines which representation should be removed, compressed, or deprioritized while other representations are retained. The goal is to exploit the complementary strengths of different representations while reducing redundant storage. Detailed visual information may be selectively discarded or compressed while a more compact long-term representation is preserved (Xiong et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026h; Wang et al., 2025c).

4.3 T3: Self-Evolving Memory

T3 Self-Evolving Memory represents a memory-centered form of inference-time learning in which experience accumulated during inference drives improvements in memory management policies. Memory therefore supports inference-time learning at two levels: accumulated experience supports the agent’s inference-time learning, while the memory system itself can also evolve through feedback-driven updates to its management policies.

The evolving policy may be realized through learned parameters (Zou et al., 2026a), symbolic rules (Bärmann et al., 2026), utility-based decision criteria (Sun et al., 2026b), or explicit procedures such as reusable retrieval strategies (Fan et al., 2026b) and executable programs (El Hattami et al., 2026).

For multimodal memory, policy evolution must account for the different roles of heterogeneous representations. A write policy determines which source observations or features should be retained and how they should be transformed into persistent records. A maintenance policy determines which representations and levels of detail should remain available as memory accumulates. A retrieval policy determines which representation or store should be searched and how evidence across representations should be coordinated. We therefore organize T3 Self-Evolving Memory methods into writing-policy, maintenance-policy, and retrieval-policy evolution.

4.3.1 Write-Policy Evolution

Write-policy evolution uses feedback to improve how raw experiences are selected and transformed into memory. Unlike a fixed write mechanism, which repeatedly applies the same admission and representation-transformation procedures, an evolving write policy adapts what information is retained and how that information is represented in response to feedback obtained during deployment.

The selection policy determines which parts of raw experience should be retained as memory records. Feedback from new interactions or completed tasks is used to adapt the policy toward retaining the most relevant parts of raw experience that are likely to support subsequent reasoning (Zou et al., 2026a). However, this adaptation introduces a key trade-off: when the task or environment changes substantially during deployment, a policy optimized for prior experience may discard important information in the new setting.

The transformation policy changes how selected multimodal evidence is converted into the target memory representation. This evolution currently operates through three main mechanisms. Representational abstraction determines the semantic granularity and level of detail preserved when raw experience is converted into an explicit record. Normalization and grounding improve temporal alignment, entity resolution, and contextual grounding across modality-specific observations before they are committed to memory. Structural construction changes how grounded evidence is organized into entities, events, attributes, relations, or graph structures. In source-linked memory, it may also adapt how derived semantic or structured records are connected to their supporting visual observations, interaction traces, timestamps, and entity identifiers. Failure traces can produce validated policy changes that repair graph construction and source-to-record mappings while preserving provenance and consistency across linked representations (Tian et al., 2026). Across these mechanisms, the central tension is to improve task relevance and representational efficiency without losing source-grounded details, temporal consistency, or cross-modal relationships needed by future tasks.

4.3.2 Maintenance-Policy Evolution

Maintenance-policy evolution uses feedback to improve how existing memory representations are retained, revised, and removed over time. The maintenance policy determines which stored representations persist and how much information is preserved during operations such as consolidation, reorganization, and forgetting. Unlike a fixed maintenance policy, an evolving policy adapts these decisions based on user feedback or accumulated evidence of downstream utility. Two main mechanisms emerge for maintenance-policy evolution.

Feedback-driven retention uses user feedback to revise which memory representations should remain available over time. When a failed memory query reveals that relevant information was previously removed, the feedback updates the retention policy so that similar information encountered in the future is retained longer (Bärmann et al., 2026). This mechanism improves future retention decisions but cannot recover information already removed unless it remains available through another linked representation. Feedback-driven representation abstraction uses feedback to determine the information to be preserved when a memory representation is being compressed. Updated relevance criteria guide subsequent grouping and summarization toward preserving information that has proved useful to the user or downstream tasks.

4.3.3 Retrieval-Policy Evolution

Retrieval-policy evolution uses feedback to improve the reusable strategies that govern memory access. Specifically, the retrieval policy determines how queries are formulated and how candidate memories are prioritized for subsequent reasoning. Existing methods primarily focus on two policy targets: search formulation and control, and memory selection and prioritization.

Search formulation and control adapt how queries are constructed and how incomplete retrieval is repaired. Successful and failed retrieval trajectories can be distilled into reusable guidance describing evidence requirements, query patterns, and corrective searches. In long-video reasoning, this guidance informs subsequent query construction over the current memory graph, while answer generation remains grounded in evidence retrieved from the current video (Fan et al., 2026b).

After searching, memory selection and prioritization determine which candidate records receive a higher probability of selection by the retrieval. In embodied memory, (Tian et al., 2026) utilizes validated rules to prioritize object records supported by direct observations, using location, recency, and links to source evidence to guide retrieval in later tasks. (Sun et al., 2026b) updates memory utility estimates from downstream feedback in clinical settings.

The evolution of memory-management policies benefits from feedback across the memory lifecycle, as errors introduced at one stage can affect later stages. Information omitted during writing or lost during maintenance cannot be recovered through improvements to the retrieval policy. A failed memory retrieval may therefore reflect earlier information loss, ineffective retrieval, or incorrect use of retrieved evidence. Distinguishing the causes of these failures motivates evaluating writing, maintenance, and retrieval jointly and targeting policy updates to the mechanisms that contribute to failure.

5 Cross-Axis Analysis

Axis I and Axis II describe different aspects of multimodal agent memory, but they interact in system design. Memory representation constrains how reliably the operations required at each management tier can be performed. T1 Static Memory requires fixed memory to be located, accessed, and reused in downstream reasoning or action. T2 Dynamic Memory further requires the correct memory units to be updated through a stable policy, verified, and synchronized across linked representations without affecting unrelated content. T3 Self-Evolving Memory adds a stronger requirement: feedback must be attributed to a memory-management decision, and the relevant writing, maintenance, or retrieval policy must evolve safely and persistently.

As the scope of persistent change expands from memory state to management policy, each tier inherits the representational bottlenecks of the preceding tier and adds another level of uncertainty. As shown in Table 1, T1 depends on preserving and accessing task-relevant information. T2 additionally depends on correctly changing and coordinating the memory state. T3 further depends on evaluating these management decisions and attributing feedback to a reusable policy component.

We therefore examine the representation requirements for T1 Static Memory, T2 Dynamic Memory, and T3 Self-Evolving Memory, followed by corpus-level patterns across the two axes.

5.1 Representation Requirements for Static Memory

T1 Static Memory imposes the simplest requirement on memory representation. Once memory has been formed, the system only needs to find and use it for downstream reasoning or action. The main representational requirement for T1 Static Memory systems is that memory formation preserves the information needed for later tasks in a form that can be effectively accessed and reused. Effective access mechanisms and retrieval indices must identify the stored context most relevant to the current query and make it available to the agent (Yu et al., 2025c; Fan et al., 2024; Yeo et al., 2026a). T1 Static Memory requires no persistent memory change: the fixed memory only needs to be accessed and reused.

5.2 Representation Requirements for Dynamic Memory

T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable management policy. The memory state changes during use, while the policy that controls these changes remains stable. Finding and using memory is no longer sufficient. The system must change the correct memory unit, preserve unrelated information, and keep dependent representations consistent. We unfold our discussion into the properties below:

Editability

We use editability to describe whether a target memory unit can be directly modified, replaced, or removed, and at what granularity the change can be applied. We use operation scope to describe all memory units, relations, indices, and behaviors affected by the operation, including both intended and unintended effects. A controlled operation should have a minimal sufficient scope: it should change the target unit and its necessary dependencies while preserving unrelated memory.

The available editing scope depends on the representation, which we categorize them as source-preserving memory and cross-represented explicit memory. Source-preserving memory allows the system to append, replace, or remove individual observations. However, a semantic error may lie in an interpretation derived from the source evidence rather than in the retained observation itself. If an agent assigns the wrong identity to a person in a video, the stored frames still record the visual input available to the agent and need not be modified. The error lies in the annotation, entity association, or derived record. Correcting it therefore requires changing the derived representation rather than the source evidence. Cross-represented explicit memory exposes facts, events, entities, attributes, and relations as separate units. These units can be changed directly (Feng et al., 2026; Yeo et al., 2026b). However, an explicit memory unit may have several dependencies. Changing an entity identity may also require changes to its attributes, event records, summaries, relations, and retrieval indices. An operation that is too narrow leaves these dependent records outdated. An operation that is too broad may change unrelated information. Latent and parametric memory is harder to edit with a controlled scope. Information may be distributed across latent states, model weights, or adapters. A state transition or optimization step can change the representation, but the system may not know which numerical components encode the target information. The update may therefore affect unrelated knowledge or behavior.

Verifiability

Verifiability asks whether the result of a memory operation can be checked for correctness. It requires a trace that connects the previous memory state, the applied operation, the supporting evidence, and the resulting state. The representation used for verification may differ from the representation being changed. A revised textual event record may need to be checked against a video segment, GUI state, audio interval, or embodied interaction trace. Explicit and source-linked memory can support this comparison through evidence identifiers and provenance links. For latent or parametric memory, direct record-level verification is usually unavailable. The system must instead use behavioral tests to check whether the intended behavior changed while unrelated behavior remained stable (Seong et al., 2025).

Reversibility

Reversibility asks whether the memory state preceding that operation can be restored. Reversal is needed when later evidence, verification, or downstream outcomes reveal that a memory operation introduced an incorrect or harmful change, such as overwriting a valid record after an erroneous entity match. Preserving the original observation alone may not be sufficient for reversing a memory operation. Regenerating a summary or structured record from that observation may not reproduce the previous state when the formation process uses a stochastic model such as an LLM. Reliable reversal therefore requires a previous version, an operation log, or an inverse operation. Explicit memory can support item-level or version-level restoration. Latent and parametric memory often relies on model checkpoints, which may also remove valid updates made after the operation being reversed.

Update propagation

Update propagation describes how the effects of a memory operation are carried from one representation to other dependent representations. This issue arises in hybrid and source-linked memory, where the same information may be stored in several forms. An operation applied to one representation may therefore require corresponding changes to the others. Cross-representation consistency describes whether these dependent representations remain aligned after the operation.

Propagation must be both complete and selective. Correcting a person’s identity may require changes to textual records, entity links, summaries, and retrieval indices, while the original image remains unchanged as source evidence. A new observation of an object’s location may update its current-state record and retrieval index while preserving earlier observations as historical evidence. Under-propagation leaves outdated or conflicting records. Over-propagation may remove valid evidence or change unrelated information. Reliable propagation, therefore, requires links between representations that refer to the same experience. These links may use timestamps, source identifiers, entity identifiers, version identifiers, or provenance relations.

The representation requirements for T2 Dynamic Memory are therefore stronger than those for T1 Static Memory. Source-preserving memory retains evidence but often lacks direct targets for semantic correction. Cross-represented explicit memory supports precise edits but requires provenance, versioning, and dependency tracking. Latent and parametric memory can be updated, but its update scope is difficult to identify and verify. Hybrid and source-linked memory supports both explicit correction and source-based verification, but it must keep its representations synchronized.

5.3 Representation Requirements for Self-Evolving Memory

The representation requirements discussed for T2 Dynamic Memory remain relevant to T3 Self-Evolving Memory. T3 introduces an additional meta-level requirement: the system must represent its memory-management policies, the decisions produced by that policy, and the feedback used to evaluate and revise it. Self-evolution therefore depends on policy addressability, policy-level feedback attribution, and persistent, validated policy revision.

Policy Addressability

For a memory-management policy to evolve, the part responsible for a recurring behavior must provide an identifiable target for revision. It may be represented explicitly as a rule, instruction, workflow, program, or retrieval specification, or implicitly in a learned module or parameter set. Explicit policy representations allow more precise revisions, whereas distributed representations make the effects of individual changes harder to isolate.

An explicit memory representation and an explicit policy representation serve different purposes. The former exposes the content being managed, whereas the latter exposes the mechanism that determines how this content is formed, maintained, and accessed. Identifiable memory items can make a state change easier to inspect, but they do not by themselves identify which part of the management policy should be revised.

Policy Evaluation and Feedback Attribution

T3 must evaluate whether outcomes reveal a recurring weakness in the memory-management policy rather than an isolated error in the memory state. This requires connecting an outcome to the memory content involved, the management decisions that shaped its availability and use, and the policy component and version that produced those decisions. A policy-evaluation record may therefore include the relevant task context, affected memory items, operations performed, retrieved content, policy version, and subsequent feedback.

This requirement extends the operation-level traceability needed in T2. In T2, a trace supports verification or reversal of a particular memory-state change. In T3, traces across interactions support policy-level attribution: determining whether repeated outcomes justify changing the reusable mechanism that selects such operations. Feedback must therefore be sufficiently informative to distinguish failures of writing, maintenance, retrieval, reasoning, and action. A task-level reward alone may reveal that the agent failed without identifying which part of memory management should change.

Axis I constrains what evidence is available for this evaluation. Explicit memory units, provenance, operation histories, and source links permit more direct inspection of management decisions. Distributed latent or parametric representations expose fewer identifiable units and therefore place greater weight on behavioral evaluation across tasks. Thus, the memory representation affects how directly the memory-management design can be evaluated.

Persistent and Validated Policy Revision

A policy revision constitutes self-evolution only when it is retained as part of the reusable memory-management process and affects subsequent memory operations. The system must therefore represent the revised policy in a form that can be stored, reapplied, and associated with later decisions. Maintaining policy versions and their evaluation histories also supports comparison, auditing, and restoration when a revision proves harmful.

Validation must assess the revised policy rather than only the memory-state change that motivated it. Correcting one record demonstrates that a particular error has been repaired, but it does not establish that the revised policy will manage future memories more effectively. Policy-level validation therefore requires subsequent, replayed, or held-out cases that test both the targeted behavior and possible regressions in other memory functions.

T3 Self-Evolving Memory requires a meta-level representation that closes the loop from policy decisions to outcomes, from outcomes to evaluation, and from evaluation to persistent and validated policy change.

5.4 Corpus-Level Patterns Across the Two Axes

Figure 8 reports the distribution of architectures across the two taxonomy axes. Each architecture is assigned to its highest supported management tier and to one representation category. Hybrid architectures form a separate category in this plot; the remaining architectures are grouped by their representation family. The incidence plots in Figures 9 and 10 separately count each representation family present within an architecture, including those in hybrid systems.

Figures 10 and 9 show that multimodal agent memory architectures concentrate in T2 Dynamic Memory across modalities and in the overall corpus, while T3 Self-Evolving Memory remains relatively rare. Of the 297 architectures, 221 (74.4%) update memory state or its management policy during operation. T2 Dynamic Memory accounts for 204 architectures (68.7% of the corpus) that update memory through stable management policies, whereas T3 Self-Evolving Memory accounts for 17 architectures (5.7%) that update their management policies based on deployment-time feedback. Stable management policies allow agents to incorporate new experience through predictable and controllable update procedures, making them the dominant approach to memory updating.

Hybrid representations help address the competing requirements of multimodal memory. Hybrid systems constitute 139 of the 297 architectures (46.8%), making them the largest representation category. Their prevalence suggests that a single representation type is often insufficient to balance representational fidelity, preservation of modality-specific detail, retrieval efficiency, and storage cost for rich multimodal experiences. Hybrid architectures are therefore the most common representational choice, but they do not dominate the landscape: many systems address narrower memory problems using the single representation type best suited to their tasks.

Compact and explicit memory artifacts are the predominant target for deployment-time policy evolution. Of the 17 T3 Self-Evolving Memory architectures, 13 are cross-represented systems, while the other 4 are hybrid systems that include an explicit representation. By contrast, to the best of our knowledge, neither the source-preserving category nor the latent or parametric category contains a T3 Self-Evolving Memory system under our definition. Explicit rules, skills, workflows, retrieval descriptions, and programs occupy a useful middle ground for deployment-time evolution: they are more compact and directly editable than detailed source observations, while remaining more inspectable and controllable than information distributed across latent states or model parameters. These properties provide identifiable targets that can be revised from feedback, validated, and reused in subsequent tasks.

The analysis above characterizes multimodal agent memory at the logical level: how experience is represented, how memory state and management policies may change, and what requirements arise from their interaction. These logical requirements must ultimately be realized by concrete runtime mechanisms. Memory access requires stored representations to be located and materialized for computation, while memory updates require dependent artifacts to remain identifiable, synchronized, and valid as state changes. Section 6 therefore examines the systems mechanisms that realize these logical memory designs under finite compute, memory, storage, and communication resources.

6 Systems Infrastructure for Multimodal Agent Memory

6.1 Scope and System Abstractions

Sections 3, 4 and 5 characterize multimodal agent memory at the logical level. Axis I determines what experience is retained and the operative representation through which it becomes available to downstream reasoning or action. Axis II determines whether the system reuses fixed memory, updates memory state through a stable policy, or evolves the memory-management policy itself. Section 5 further shows that these choices impose requirements on editability, verifiability, reversibility, and update propagation. This section examines how those logical representations, operations, and requirements are realized through physical storage and runtime execution under finite compute, memory, storage, and communication resources. These distinctions organize the infrastructure discussion without introducing an additional axis of the memory taxonomy.

Logical memory denotes the experience-derived state defined in Section 2, whose operative representation determines its classification in Section 3. When the representation exposes an independently identifiable unit, such as an image, event record, graph node, or trajectory, we call that unit a logical memory object. This does not assume that every latent state or parameter update exposes equally addressable semantic units. A physical realization comprises the concrete records, tensors, parameter modules, replicas, and auxiliary indices that store this state or make it accessible. For example, PixelRAG indexes screenshot tiles using visual embeddings but supplies the retrieved screenshots to the VLM as source evidence (Wang et al., 2026j). An index or storage format therefore supports access to memory without necessarily defining its operative representation.

Materialized execution state is the runtime form through which selected memory participates in current computation. Materialization may assemble textual or visual context, construct model-compatible features or latent tokens, restore KV states, or activate an experience-specific parameter module. These are overlapping roles rather than disjoint storage classes: a retained tensor can be both an operative memory representation and an artifact used during execution. Mem-W, for example, constructs latent tokens from retrieved trajectories and expired in-session history for subsequent agent decisions (Zhang et al., 2026b). Conversely, an ordinary request-local activation or cache does not become agent memory merely because it occupies storage or accelerates decoding. The relevant criterion is its deliberate role in retaining experience for later reasoning or action. Such reuse can occur within a trajectory: TRAM carries auxiliary recurrent states across reasoning steps while resetting them for each input (Liu et al., 2026h). Accordingly, persistence here concerns the intended reuse horizon; it does not by itself imply cross-session storage or durability after a process or machine failure.

Logical and physical lifecycles must consequently be distinguished. The tier migration discussed in Section 4.2.4 changes a memory’s temporal or functional role, whereas moving an unchanged artifact from accelerator HBM to host DRAM changes its residency. Likewise, evicting a reconstructible cache or redundant replica need not forget the underlying experience. This separation is conditional on preserving the required information: deleting the last recoverable copy or applying irreversible lossy transformations can affect what the agent can subsequently recall. Physical cache replacement alone does not establish T2 memory-state adaptation, nor does workload-responsive scheduling alone establish T3 evolution of a memory-management policy.

Our coverage therefore includes both systems that retain multimodal experience and transferable mechanisms from model serving, storage, and retrieval. InferCept’s treatment of tool-interrupted KV state and SGLang’s prefix reuse provide useful runtime mechanisms, but neither mechanism alone specifies how an agent forms or revises experience-derived memory (Abhyankar et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). We use such work to explain infrastructure capabilities and their limits, rather than treating every cache optimization as a multimodal memory architecture.

Figure 11 organizes this systems view. Sections 6.2 and 6.3 examine where artifacts reside and the cost of moving or reconstructing them. Section 6.4 separates evidence relevance, execution-state compatibility, and scheduling benefit. Section 6.5 considers transformations between retained experience and active computation, while Section 6.6 examines ownership, visibility, and compatibility across updates. The remaining integration challenges are discussed in Section 8.5.

6.2 Physical Storage and Residency

Long-running agents can accumulate substantially more historical state than an individual request consumes, motivating a separation between retained memory and its active working set (Omri et al., 2026). ReKV provides a multimodal example: it retains video KV caches beyond the current processing window in RAM or on disk, then loads the caches of a query-relevant subset of frames for question answering (Di et al., 2025). Under a bounded retrieval budget, retained history can therefore grow without a proportional increase in the state loaded for each answer. Residency management determines which artifacts occupy each storage tier, how long physical copies remain there, and when to promote, demote, replicate, or evict them.

Storage tiers offer different capacity and access-cost trade-offs. Accelerator HBM accommodates state used by active inference; host DRAM can retain inactive state without occupying GPU capacity; and local SSDs extend retention beyond host memory. ReKV illustrates the latter two options for historical video KV (Di et al., 2025). Placement also extends beyond a single machine. Mooncake pools cluster-wide DRAM and SSD resources for shared KV retention, while ITME uses disaggregated, SSD-backed CXL-hybrid memory to expand prefix-cache capacity (Qin et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2026). Network-attached pools and CXL-attached expansion provide different access paths, not interchangeable latency guarantees. Moreover, raw media, retrieval embeddings, model-consumed features, and KV states derived from the same experience need not be co-located: their sizes, reuse horizons, and reconstruction costs differ.

Tool calls make retention time an explicit decision. InferCept compares Preserve, Swap, and Discard: keeping intercepted KV on the GPU, moving it to host memory, or reconstructing it after resumption (Abhyankar et al., 2024). Continuum adds a time-to-live (TTL) to GPU retention, balancing the cost of occupying capacity against avoided reload or recomputation and subsequent queueing delay (Li et al., 2025a). TTL expiration ends protection under the scheduler’s rules; it does not make the remembered evidence semantically obsolete. MORI instead ranks complete agent programs by recent relative idleness, retaining busier programs in HBM and more-idle programs in DRAM (Xia et al., 2026b). Its sticky placement changes tiers when capacity pressure requires demotion or available HBM permits promotion, avoiding migration at every tool-call boundary. These mechanisms use different signals—interruption cost, retention time, and program activity—to balance occupancy against resumption overhead.

Distributed reuse introduces a second placement dimension: which nodes retain an artifact and how many copies are maintained. Mooncake tracks cache locations and supports replication so that frequently accessed KV blocks can be available on multiple workers (Qin et al., 2025). Local replicas reduce repeated remote access but increase aggregate storage; shared pools reduce the need to duplicate every artifact but expose remote-transfer costs. For multimodal memory, these decisions can be made separately for source media and expensive derived states. They must also respect the distinction between sharing an observation and reusing its computation: identical historical evidence does not imply that its KV state is compatible with every consuming context.

The central residency trade-off is therefore not simply hot versus cold storage. It combines expected reuse time, state size, reconstruction cost, concurrent demand, and access locality. Program admission and worker selection interact with these decisions, as discussed in Section 6.4. The cost of implementing a residency change depends on the transfer and restoration mechanisms considered next.

6.3 Data Movement, Compression, and Reconstruction

A retained artifact is not necessarily ready for execution. Storage access, interconnect transfer, decompression, and layout conversion can delay its use even when lookup succeeds. These costs concern the restoration path; they are distinct from deciding where an artifact should reside or whether it is compatible with the current request.

Pipelining reduces the transfer latency exposed on the critical path. CachedAttention uses layer-wise preloading and asynchronous saving to overlap KV access with computation (Gao et al., 2024). Across nodes, Mooncake supports asynchronous transfers over RDMA-capable infrastructure and streams newly produced KV toward decode workers during prefill (Qin et al., 2025). Buffering enables overlap but consumes additional memory, and concurrent transfers can compete with inference for bandwidth. Consequently, an asynchronous interface alone does not guarantee that restoration is hidden.

Compression and partial recomputation offer complementary ways to reduce transferred bytes. CacheGen combines quantization and entropy coding with chunked streaming, overlapping transmission with codec decoding (Liu et al., 2024a). Cake concurrently recomputes from the beginning of a reusable prefix and loads cached KV from its end, adapting the division of work to available computation and I/O resources (Jin et al., 2025b). The trade-off is therefore among transferred bytes, codec work, temporary storage, and recomputation. Lossy compression additionally affects approximation quality. In particular, a compact transport bitstream need not occupy proportionally less HBM after it is decoded into inference tensors.

Multimodal and agent workloads provide additional overlap windows. MPIC loads cached image state while computing missing image caches; this overlap is distinct from its selective recomputation for contextual reuse (Zhao et al., 2025b). TokenCake exploits tool-call intervals for opportunistic asynchronous offload and predictive upload, and initiates immediate upload when a tool returns earlier than predicted (Bian et al., 2027). Workflow-informed prefetching also uses anticipated agent execution, as discussed for KVFlow in Section 6.4. These mechanisms reduce exposed restoration cost when sufficient independent work is available, but short intervals, prediction errors, and contention can leave transfers on the critical path. Completing a transfer establishes availability, not reuse validity.

6.4 Indexing, Reuse, and Scheduling

The request-time control path separates three questions: which memory is relevant, whether a retained execution artifact is compatible, and whether reusing it is worthwhile. A logical-memory index identifies accessible evidence or experience; an execution-state index identifies potentially reusable computation associated with concrete inputs and execution dependencies. A hit in the first does not imply a hit in the second, and neither hit alone determines the best execution plan.

Logical-memory access reflects the organization of retained experience. M3-Agent combines semantic similarity with timestamp-based sequential retrieval and entity-based associative retrieval over text, image, and audio memory (Long et al., 2026). DynaMem couples language-based localization with a spatial-semantic map and can retrieve the latest image associated with a selected voxel (Liu et al., 2025b). These access paths exploit temporal order, entity links, spatial structure, and modality-bearing evidence. Their results identify what the agent should inspect; they do not certify the reusability of tensors previously computed from those objects.

Execution-state indexing instead exploits computational dependencies. SGLang’s RadixAttention organizes token prefixes and their KV states in a radix tree, with image hashes representing multimodal inputs within that indexing scheme (Zheng et al., 2024). Exact-prefix reuse requires matching the relevant input prefix and computational configuration, including positions and model dependencies; an image hash by itself is insufficient. Prompt Cache enables modular reuse within an explicitly defined positional schema, whereas CacheBlend selectively recomputes cached states to restore cross-chunk contextualization (Gim et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025a). MPIC similarly addresses image-context reuse through position handling and selective recomputation (Zhao et al., 2025b). These methods should not be treated as equivalent guarantees: schema-constrained reuse and quality-evaluated approximate reconstruction differ from exact reuse of an unchanged prefix.

Scheduling determines how compatible reuse opportunities interact with resource demand. SGLang orders requests to exploit common cached prefixes, while Preble jointly considers prefix reuse and load balancing when dispatching requests across workers (Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025). Reusing a prefix on an overloaded worker can be less attractive than recomputing it elsewhere. For retrieval-mediated requests, evidence relevance governs what enters computation, whereas cache locality concerns where that computation can run efficiently. Neither should silently substitute for the other.

Agent execution provides signals beyond individual requests. ThunderAgent treats a complete agent program as a scheduling unit, using execution phase and context footprint to pause or restore programs under memory pressure (Kang et al., 2026). Its global waiting queue permits paused programs to resume on a worker with available capacity, rather than requiring their original placement. KVFlow exploits an exposed Agent Step Graph to estimate steps-to-execution, prioritize fixed-prefix KV nodes, and prefetch upcoming state from CPU to GPU (Pan et al., 2025). Its workflow-level reuse signal depends on an exposed graph, which may include conditional branches. Together with MORI’s tier-level admission control (Xia et al., 2026b), these designs connect execution readiness to cache retention and capacity allocation.

Here, admission concerns requests, programs, or physical cache entries, rather than the semantic decision to write an observation into logical memory. A useful reuse decision must account for validation, transfer, reconstruction, queueing, and displaced work, not just the amount of cached state. Section 6.5 examines the transformations selected by this control path, and Section 6.6 examines how subsequent updates affect their eligibility for reuse.

6.5 Materialization and Write-back

Materialization and write-back implement the two directions of the logical memory lifecycle described in Sections 3 and 4. On the read path, materialization converts a selected logical memory representation into model-consumable context, features, latent states, or parameter modules for current computation. On the write path, observations, execution history, or completed trajectories are transformed into persistent state that can subsequently participate in memory formation or management. The systems concern here is therefore not what should be remembered or updated, but when these transformations execute, what artifacts they produce, and what preparation and consumption costs they impose.

Textual and source-level inputs have different preparation costs. PixelRAG renders and indexes screenshot tiles during datastore construction, then supplies retrieved pixels to a VLM. Downsampling before reading reduces visual-token demand without rebuilding the datastore or retrieval index (Wang et al., 2026j). FOLIO supplies compact semantic records and can recover linked keyframes when its relevance criterion indicates insufficient grounding (Fan et al., 2026a). Reopening images may recover details missing from an abstraction, but incurs visual encoding and additional model input. Storage compression, visual-token reduction, and downstream attention cost are therefore distinct efficiency measures.

Latent-token and KV-based paths move work across different boundaries. Mem-W uses a visual–textual encoder and a Q-Former-based compressor to produce a fixed number of soft memory tokens per selected trajectory segment (Zhang et al., 2026b). The limit bounds expansion per segment, not the total cost of encoding or selecting multiple segments. ReKV instead constructs video KV incrementally before a question arrives and binds retrieved blocks into question-answering attention (Di et al., 2025). Its retrieved tokens receive consecutive positions rather than their original video positions. This is part of a specific attention and positional scheme, not evidence that arbitrary cached tensors can be reused after context changes. Latent compression pays preparation work to reduce the model-facing input, whereas KV precomputation moves part of that work ahead of the query and retains the resulting tensors.

Parametric memory follows a further path that is not captured by context insertion alone. Frames2LoRA generates a video-specific LoRA adapter from video-conditioned representations through a trained hypernetwork; subsequent questions use the adapted model without replaying the original visual tokens (Suri et al., 2026). From a runtime perspective, the relevant artifacts are the generated parameter module and the backbone to which it is attached. The corresponding costs include adapter production, retention, loading, and activation, rather than only context length. This complements the parametric representation discussion in Section 3.3.2 without treating ordinary pretrained model weights as experience-derived agent memory.

Write-back must likewise distinguish reuse horizons. Mem-W carries expired interaction history forward as compressed latent context, while MementoGUI both compacts older working-memory entries and uses a separate Episodic Writer to construct source-linked records for later episodes (Zhang et al., 2026b; Zeng et al., 2026). In-session compaction preserves task progress; episodic write-back creates a cross-episode retrieval artifact. Both can retain experience for later use, but only episodic write-back crosses that external episodic-storage boundary. Neither description alone specifies crash durability. Producing summaries, organizing visual crops, and constructing retrieval embeddings also consume resources before later reads can benefit.

Reasoning history can become either recurrent state or procedural experience. TRAM pools completed-step activations into fast and slow recurrent states that influence later reasoning within the same input (Liu et al., 2026h). RRM instead distills completed retrieval trajectories and feedback into procedural records, excluding historical answers and video-specific facts; retrieved procedures guide subsequent evidence acquisition rather than being inserted as factual answer context (Fan et al., 2026b). These paths differ in both what persists and the model interface through which it is reused.

Write-back may produce linked artifacts asynchronously. FOLIO builds semantic records associated with retained keyframes while a short-term visual buffer supplies recent evidence; M2A maintains raw message records alongside editable semantic observations linked by evidence identifiers (Fan et al., 2026a; Feng et al., 2026). Retaining these links enables later source recovery but entails constructing and maintaining both abstractions and supporting artifacts. The cost of memory therefore spans construction, retrieval, and consumption, rather than stored size alone (Omri et al., 2026). Publication and update coordination across these artifacts are considered next.

6.6 Consistency and Coordination

Consistency and coordination provide the systems support for the T2 representation requirements identified in Section 5.2. When memory is updated, later reads may encounter different record versions, physical replicas, or derived execution states. Editability requires the system to identify the affected logical object and its physical realizations; verifiability requires provenance and version information connecting the update to supporting evidence; reversibility requires an earlier version, operation log, checkpoint, or reconstructible source; and update propagation requires dependent artifacts to be refreshed or invalidated. Coordination determines when these changes become visible and which versions or derivatives remain eligible for use. Deciding whether new evidence should revise a belief remains a memory-management question, whereas publishing the selected revision consistently across access paths is a systems question.

Update ownership and evidence identity provide a starting point. M2A gives its MemoryManager exclusive read–write access to the memory bank and links semantic observations to supporting messages (Feng et al., 2026). This identifies an application-level owner and evidence trail, not a distributed transaction protocol. When a dependency changes, the associated derivation must be refreshed or its compatibility re-established before it is used for a request requiring the revised state. Historical queries may still use an earlier version when its temporal scope and access permissions permit. This selective treatment avoids invalidating unchanged source evidence merely because an interpretation has been corrected.

Publication rules determine what readers see while writes proceed. FOLIO excludes segment records still being written and instead answers from completed memory and recent visual context (Fan et al., 2026a). Manu coordinates vector-store subscribers through timestamped logs and time-tick progress markers, allowing queries to wait for a configured freshness level (Guo et al., 2022). These mechanisms operate at different boundaries: application records in the former and indexed data with row-level ACID support in the latter. Their guarantees do not automatically compose into atomic publication across separately maintained media, semantic records, retrieval indices, and model-side states.

Shared execution state also requires lifetime and aliasing control. Mooncake tracks prefix-dependent cache blocks and their replicas and protects blocks used by ongoing requests from eviction (Qin et al., 2025). Within an inference engine, vLLM uses reference-counted block sharing and copy-on-write when a sequence extends a shared KV block (Kwon et al., 2023). These mechanisms prevent premature reclamation and interference between branches, but do not determine whether the underlying memory has become stale. Similarly, Manu’s deletion bitmaps suppress deleted vectors in search before segment-index rebuilding (Guo et al., 2022). Read exclusion, storage reclamation, and invalidation of derived representations are separate operations.

Authorization imposes another visibility boundary. Collaborative Memory separates private and shared fragments and uses provenance and a current access graph to filter retrieval as permissions change (Rezazadeh et al., 2025). This controls exposure through its retrieval interface; it does not demonstrate retroactive removal of information already materialized in another agent’s context or KV state. Authorization is consequently distinct from copy-on-write: one governs who may consume an artifact, while the other protects shared physical state against a branch’s mutations.

Compatibility can change even when source observations do not. FastFill aligns embeddings across model updates and prioritizes partial backfilling using alignment uncertainty (Jaeckle et al., 2023). This addresses retrieval features, not arbitrary model-consumed latent memory. DroidSpeak selectively recomputes layer groups when reusing KV across profiled fine-tuned model variants (Liu et al., 2026k); its scope is model-pair-specific, and substantial distribution drift can degrade quality. Compatibility therefore depends on the producer, consumer, and validated transformation, not source identity alone.

The analyzed mechanisms coordinate particular records, retrieval views, or execution blocks. Their combination exposes trade-offs among freshness, read latency, sharing, bookkeeping, and reconstruction.
