A retained historical observation can remain valid after a current-state record changes, while an unchanged physical cache can become incompatible with a new consumer. Establishing explicit guarantees across these boundaries is the integration problem developed in Section 8.5. Sections 6.2 and 6.6 do not introduce new memory types; they characterize the runtime conditions under which the representation and management choices in Sections 3, 4 and 5 can be served efficiently, consistently, and within finite resources.

7 Evaluation and Applications

Section 5 analyzes how representation constrains memory management, while Section 6 examines how the resulting designs are realized at runtime. This section characterizes how multimodal memory systems are evaluated and what functions memory serves in their applications. Section 7.1 defines the capabilities that memory benchmarks attempt to measure, Section 7.2 characterizes the 82 benchmark records by evaluation setting, Section 7.3 describes the functions memory serves in deployed systems, and Section 7.4 reports what those benchmarks do and do not exercise. What the field should do about the gaps recorded here is argued in Section 8.

7.1 Evaluation Dimensions for Multimodal Agent Memory

End-task accuracy alone cannot establish whether an agent has used memory: a correct output may follow from the current context or parametric knowledge, while an error may arise during memory formation, access, maintenance, or utilization. Recent benchmarks therefore increasingly evaluate not only task outcomes, but also the evidence and state transitions supporting them (Ren et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026c). Accordingly, Table 2 characterizes each benchmark through shared memory capabilities, modality-specific requirements, and evaluation settings. The six shared dimensions capture three stages of memory use.

These dimensions are modality-independent: they characterize whether memory preserves sufficient evidence, remains valid under change, and contributes to downstream decisions.

Shared dimensions alone, however, cannot express the internal structure that must survive within each modality. Image-memory benchmarks therefore distinguish fine-grained visual-detail retention (FG), entity tracking across observations (ET), and visual state-change tracking (VC). Video benchmarks add temporal localization (TL), temporal-relation reasoning over event order and duration (TR), and multi-event evidence integration (ME) (Zhang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026i). Audio and speech benchmarks require speaker tracking (SP), acoustic-cue retention (AC), and repair persistence (RP). SP tests whether a memory preserves who spoke across turns or sessions; AC tests whether it retains non-lexical evidence such as prosody, vocal style, and background sound; and RP tests whether spoken feedback or later evidence produces a persistent correction rather than a transient response (Xie et al., 2026c; Jiang et al., 2026b; Chattopadhyay et al., 2026). GUI evaluation emphasizes persistent interface state (GS), associations between actions and resulting states (AO), and reuse of experience across sessions (XR) (Liu et al., 2026d). Embodied benchmarks instead require spatial memory (SM), object-state tracking under partial observability (OS), and task-state or progress tracking (TS) (Hu et al., 2025a; Yadav et al., 2026). These dimensions expose representational failures that long-range or cross-modal labels cannot: an agent may retain an event while losing its precise time, remember an object while failing to preserve its location, or recall a GUI action without the state transition it produced.

The capability annotations should be interpreted together with the benchmark setup recorded in Table 2. The data source distinguishes real, synthetic, simulated, and hybrid settings, which differ in perceptual complexity, environmental control, and the availability of counterfactual conditions. The task field identifies whether memory supports question answering, retrieval, localization, generation, action, planning, learning, or mapping. The ground-truth field records what can be verified, including answers, supporting evidence, regions, timestamps, environment states, actions, provenance, and reliability labels. Answer-only supervision evaluates end-task correctness but provides limited evidence that the intended memory was used. By contrast, evidence, region, timestamp, and provenance annotations support more direct evaluation of memory grounding, while state and action supervision connect memory to interactive behavior. These setup dimensions therefore determine how precisely a benchmark can attribute success or failure to memory, even when two benchmarks nominally cover the same capability.

These dimensions also connect benchmark coverage to the taxonomy introduced earlier. CE and the modality-specific dimensions primarily specify the evidence, attributes, and relations that memory formation must preserve and make accessible, and therefore connect most directly to Axis I. LE, TL, ME, and XR probe the storage, access, and reuse of fixed memory and therefore align with T1 Static Memory, whereas SC, CF, VC, GS, AO, OS, and TS can expose demands for state maintenance or revision under changing observations and therefore inform evaluation of T2 Dynamic Memory. Offline reconstruction of a state history, however, does not by itself establish deployment-time memory updating. UQ and MA primarily evaluate memory utilization through evidence sufficiency and action selection. None of these labels alone establishes T3 Self-Evolving Memory, which requires deployment feedback to produce persistent changes to a reusable memory-management policy. This mapping supports the lifecycle-based coverage analysis in Section 7.4.

7.2 Benchmark Landscape Across Modalities

Table 2 organizes 82 selected benchmark resources and evaluation protocols by their evaluation setting. The selection includes dedicated memory tests and broader tasks used to evaluate systems that retain and reuse multimodal experience. Such tasks can reveal the contribution of memory even when their scores also depend on perception, reasoning, planning, or execution. Selected text-only and semantic-state protocols provide comparisons for shared memory functions; they do not establish visual or acoustic retention. Inclusion therefore indicates evaluation relevance, while the capability annotations describe what each protocol directly or indirectly measures. Beyond differences in sensory input, these groups vary in the experience that must persist, the horizon over which it is reused, and the supervision available to verify its contribution.

Legend. Modalities and applications denote areas receiving substantive discussion rather than isolated citations. Representation families and memory-management tiers are mapped to our taxonomy for consistent comparison. S: source- and modality-specific representations; E: cross-represented explicit memory; L/P: internalized latent or parametric memory; H: hybrid or source-linked composition.

7.2.1 Image Memory

Image benchmarks typically treat memory as a collection of visual episodes associated with dialogue, time, location, or personal context. Their horizons range from multi-turn image sequences to persistent personal archives, with question answering and retrieval as the dominant tasks. These resources differ in whether evaluation uses images directly or substitutes textual descriptions, as well as in the stages of the memory lifecycle they exercise.

LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) evaluates long-term conversational memory through question answering, event summarization, and multimodal dialogue generation. Its conversations include shared images, but the original QA and summarization experiments replace images with captions; images are used directly only in dialogue generation.

Evidence-centered benchmarks provide the clearest tests of visual persistence. Memory-QA (Jiang et al., 2025b) evaluates recall over real-world multimodal records, requiring temporal or location cues and evidence distributed across multiple memories. DISBench (Deng et al., 2026) instead evaluates context-aware retrieval and localization within interconnected visual histories, while MemLens (Ren et al., 2026) stresses whether fine-grained visual evidence survives long-term storage and retrieval.

Personalized and conversational benchmarks extend evaluation from evidence access to memory validity. LCMP (Hong et al., 2026) and ATM-Bench (Mei et al., 2026) distribute user-specific attributes and references across multiple sources and sessions, requiring the agent to track both persistent and changing information. MemEye (Guo et al., 2026b) evaluates image-grounded histories and visual state changes, while Mem-Gallery (Bei et al., 2026) and H2HMem (Zhu et al., 2026b) additionally test conflicting records and insufficient evidence. These benchmarks test whether retrieved memories remain current and mutually consistent, although updates are usually defined by curated histories rather than by an evolving memory-management policy. MemLeak (Wang and Zhang, 2026) examines a complementary requirement: whether facts requested for deletion remain recoverable from retained text or images.

A group connects image memory to action or source verification. SMMBench (Chai et al., 2026) distributes evidence across conversations, screenshots, images, tables, and documents, and provides answer, evidence, and provenance supervision for memory-grounded decisions. EMemBench (Li et al., 2026k) similarly introduces state or action consequences, but such supervision remains uncommon. Conversational benchmarks span broader dialogue evaluation and explicit memory tasks: MMDU (Liu et al., 2024b) evaluates multi-image, multi-turn response quality, whereas MMRC (Xue et al., 2025) includes memory recall, image management, and information updates. Their aggregate scores nevertheless combine memory with other dialogue capabilities. Across these settings, supervision remains predominantly answer- and evidence-based, while provenance, state, reliability, and action labels appear only in a smaller subset. Current image evaluation therefore covers fine-grained evidence retention, entity continuity, and visual state change more thoroughly than extended interaction or adaptive memory use. Provenance and behavioral verification also remain comparatively underdeveloped.

7.2.2 Video Memory

Video-memory evaluation has expanded from offline retrieval over completed recordings to causally constrained streaming and interactive assistance, but it remains dominated by readout-style question answering. We group current benchmarks into three evaluation regimes: fixed-recording or lifelog recall, causal streaming evaluation, and future-oriented interactive assistance. Although all three require access to past video, they differ in whether evidence is available as a completed record, arrives incrementally, or must influence subsequent interaction.

Fixed-recording and lifelog benchmarks provide the clearest tests of long-range temporal access. M3-Bench (Long et al., 2026) and HippoVlog (Lin et al., 2026d) cover extended audiovisual streams, while EgoLifeQA (Yang et al., 2025a) uses week-long multimodal egocentric records to support event recall, personalized question answering, and recommendation. EgoMonth (Chen et al., 2026f) extends the horizon to month-scale experience, and EgoMem (Zuo et al., 2025) emphasizes backtracking through long videos. EgoMemReason (Wang et al., 2026l) further separates entity, event, and behavioral memory. LVOmniBench (Tao et al., 2026) broadens this setting beyond egocentric data by requiring joint reasoning over long-form audio and video. These benchmarks are strong tests of temporal localization and long-range evidence retrieval, with answers established primarily through timestamps or supporting evidence, but they usually assume that the relevant video history is already available as a completed record.

Streaming evaluation introduces causal evidence availability. VStream-QA (Zhang et al., 2025b) and StreamingBench (Lin et al., 2026b) ask questions while the video continues to arrive, whereas StreamBench (Xiong et al., 2025) adds multi-round interaction over hierarchically maintained short- and long-term records. Causal access makes these benchmarks closer to deployment, but does not by itself establish that a model maintains or revises a persistent memory state. Multi-view benchmarks add a distinct challenge: memory must align temporally related evidence across agents, cameras, or viewpoints rather than retrieve from a single chronological stream. MA-EgoQA (Kim et al., 2026) constructs a shared history from synchronized egocentric streams and requires the model to identify and combine agent-specific evidence, while EgoExoMem (Liu et al., 2026i) introduces cross-view temporal and spatial dependencies. These settings therefore test distributed perspective and evidence fusion, not merely access to a longer video, although they still treat memory chiefly as a retained record to be queried rather than as a state that must be actively maintained.

A smaller group evaluates whether video memory supports future behavior. VideoWebArena (Jang et al., 2025) tests factual and skill retention from tutorials during subsequent web tasks, scoring intermediate answers and final environment states. Because video-derived information can remain in context, these scores do not isolate memory-management quality. RIVER Bench (Shi et al., 2026b) and StreamArena (Zhang et al., 2026c) combine historical recall with live or proactive responses under real-time constraints, while StreamMemBench (Liu et al., 2026e) tests whether observed evidence, feedback, and prior interaction are reused in a later task. SLVMBench (Yang et al., 2026) further asks agents to extract procedural knowledge from recorded experience and apply it to a live stream. These tasks move beyond retrospective recall toward stateful assistance, but still mainly test whether prior experience is reused, not whether deployment feedback changes the memory-management policy itself.

Across these settings, supervision remains predominantly answer-, evidence-, and timestamp-based. Overall, video benchmarks evaluate temporal localization, long-range event relations, and multi-event integration more thoroughly than most other modalities. However, conflict resolution, unanswerable queries, and memory-grounded action remain less common in Figure 12; source-level provenance and feedback-driven policy change are also weakly evaluated. This gap contrasts with the architectural trend in Figure 8: memory systems commonly update state, yet video benchmarks rarely verify whether deployment feedback produces persistent improvements in the memory-management policy.

7.2.3 Audio and Speech Memory

Audio and speech occupy a small but differentiated part of the benchmark landscape. Existing evaluations span persistent voice-grounded conversational memory, memory over streaming audiovisual experience, retrieval from a fixed long-form recording, and short-horizon speech state carried or revised across turns. These audio-based settings exercise different parts of the memory lifecycle; text-only preference protocols provide a separate comparison.

ChatMem-Bench, introduced with VoiceMem (Xie et al., 2026c), evaluates long-horizon speech memory using 316 questions over 53 hours of dialogue. Human-curated synthetic histories support tasks covering information updates, abstention, persona, affective attribution, speaker association, and non-lexical acoustic evidence. Its published category scores support direct SC, UQ, SP, and AC coverage, but only indirect CF and RP coverage: the construction pipeline includes contradictions, while a dedicated persistent spoken-repair protocol is not specified. The paper defers detailed annotation methodology to a follow-up report. EgoMem (Yao et al., 2025b) instead combines face and voice identity with asynchronously managed facts, preferences, and social relations for later personalized dialogue.

Streaming audiovisual benchmarks broaden the horizon but make audio attribution less clean. M3-Bench, TeleEgo, and Video-SALMONN S retain or evaluate audiovisual experience over long streams, yet their video-centred tasks rarely isolate speaker, prosodic, or non-speech acoustic retention (Long et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2026a). Fixed-recording benchmarks provide more controlled audio evidence: PlanRAG-Audio and LongAudioQA evaluate planned retrieval from long recordings, while ChronosAudio and AudioMarathon stress length generalization and temporal reasoning (Someki et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026b; He et al., 2025a; Gong et al., 2025). Because their memory remains fixed after formation, these settings primarily evaluate access and reuse in T1 Static Memory rather than cross-session memory updating.

Interactive ASR supplies a narrower form of state change. Agentic ASR evaluates whether spoken feedback repairs a transcription state, whereas Beyond Fresh Starts carries or rolls back acoustic and linguistic state across utterance boundaries (Jiang et al., 2026b; Chattopadhyay et al., 2026). CarMem (Kirmayr et al., 2025) provides a text-only comparison for preference extraction, retrieval, and maintenance. Its voice-assistant application does not make these experiments tests of acoustic memory. Current benchmarks therefore cover acoustic retention, long-range retrieval, speaker association, and repair separately, but rarely combine cross-session acoustic memory, conflicting spoken evidence, explicit revision, and memory-grounded action.

7.2.4 GUI Memory

GUI benchmarks occupy a compact but functionally differentiated part of the evaluation landscape. Existing settings span cross-step state retention, cross-session experience reuse, personalized and proactive interaction, and controlled diagnosis of visual memory. All reuse prior interface experience, but differ in whether memory must preserve a transient state, recover an action outcome, transfer a workflow, or retain visual evidence unavailable from text alone.

MemGUI-Bench (Liu et al., 2026d) provides the broadest direct evaluation of mobile-agent memory. Its tasks span multiple applications and use mirrored interactions to separate within-session retention from cross-session improvement, while hierarchical evaluation measures memory fidelity, learning effectiveness, and execution efficiency. MementoGUI-Bench (Zeng et al., 2026) instead formulates long-horizon GUI execution as a memory-control problem: working memory preserves task-relevant interface events and localized visual evidence, whereas episodic memory retrieves reusable trajectories. Together, these benchmarks evaluate GUI-state tracking, action–outcome associations, and experience reuse through regions, task progress, and action supervision.

Personalized and controlled settings test complementary aspects of state maintenance. KnowU-Bench (Chen et al., 2026e) hides the user profile and requires agents to infer preferences from behavioral histories, request missing information, and calibrate proactive intervention in an interactive mobile environment. Its task scores evaluate the use of history in personalized assistance, while also depending on preference inference, interaction, and execution. Memory-World (Wang et al., 2026b), introduced with STAMP, programmatically controls what transient interface information must be stored and later reused, enabling state- and action-verified evaluation in a simulated environment. DataScope (Liu et al., 2026b) combines synthetic task data with real mobile applications in 96 cross-page and cross-application workflows. Terminal success, app-level progress, and Scope-F1 verify which required operations were completed and which distractors were modified from the resulting application states; they do not provide expert action-sequence ground truth or evaluate cross-session reuse. Such benchmarks improve experimental control, although their synthetic states do not fully reproduce the variability of real applications.

DMV-Bench (Tang et al., 2026c) isolates visual memory more directly by injecting pixel-specific incidental cues into products visited across autonomous shopping sessions. Textual descriptions cannot recover the relevant cue, and successful navigation therefore depends on retaining and retrieving visual evidence with its source provenance. Current GUI evaluation consequently provides strong coverage of long-range state tracking, action outcomes, and memory-grounded execution. It remains weaker on conflicting histories, unanswerable or unsafe requests, robustness to interface change, and persistent evolution of memory-management policies. Moreover, endpoint task success alone may still fail to identify whether an error arose during memory formation, retrieval, or action selection.

7.2.5 Embodied Memory

Embodied-memory benchmarks assess whether agents can retain and use experience while navigating, mapping, and manipulating partially observable environments. Because an agent’s actions affect both the environment and the observations available later, memory must preserve spatial structure, maintain object and task states, and associate actions with their consequences. Existing benchmarks can be organized into three complementary regimes: navigation and mapping, memory-dependent manipulation, and long-horizon stateful interaction.

Navigation and mapping benchmarks primarily assess spatial persistence. FindingDory (Yadav et al., 2026) requires agents to retrieve prior visual experience for subsequent navigation and action in tasks that can be procedurally extended to longer horizons, whereas 3DMem-Bench (Hu et al., 2025a) evaluates long-term spatiotemporal question answering, scene captioning, and task execution in dynamic multi-room environments. SpaMEM (Liao et al., 2026) isolates action-conditioned revision of spatial beliefs, while HIOcc (Zhu et al., 2026a) evaluates local occupancy prediction and causal room- and building-level mapping. HIOcc measures map accuracy, online stability, and revisit consistency in static scenes; these support direct spatial-memory coverage but only partial state-change and object-state coverage, without task-progress or downstream-action evaluation. FindingDory, 3DMem-Bench, and SpaMEM additionally assess object histories or updates. Spatial regions, maps, and environment states provide supervision beyond terminal task success.

Other embodied settings assess experience reuse through planning or active perception. MEMORA-Bench (Yu et al., 2026d) pairs recall over participant-specific egocentric histories with generated plans for observed and novel goals. Its explicit information-not-available controls directly evaluate UQ, while plan-order, object-coverage, and preference scores evaluate prospective memory use; spatial, object-state, and task-progress tracking are only indirectly covered by these aggregate tasks. APRS (Tang et al., 2026b) evaluates sequential viewpoint selection and target segmentation within static panoramas, scoring search success, efficiency, and mask quality. Expert action trajectories support training rather than serving as benchmark action ground truth. SIS-Bench (Zou et al., 2026b) combines landmark and action recall with spatial reasoning and multiple-choice path planning over UAV videos. Its planning answers provide indirect MA coverage, not evidence of executed control or online task-progress tracking.

Manipulation benchmarks assess whether policies preserve action-relevant history. LIBERO-Mem (Chung et al., 2026) introduces non-Markovian tasks that require object histories beyond the current observation, with object masks, instance identities, and subgoal annotations. MIKASA-Robo (Cherepanov et al., 2026), evaluated here in its simulated RGB+joints setting, tests delayed object recall, spatial tracking, and sequential action. RMBench (Chen et al., 2026d) and ReMemBench (Shah et al., 2026) provide controlled memory-dependent manipulation tasks. RoboMME (Dai et al., 2026) evaluates temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory in vision–language–action policies, while RoboMemArena (Lei et al., 2026) extends evaluation to longer tasks with subtask and keyframe annotations and paired real-world tasks. State- and action-level supervision provides direct evidence for memory-grounded action (MA), although endpoint success cannot distinguish memory failures from errors in perception, planning, or control.

Long-horizon and cross-session benchmarks evaluate whether memory remains valid as world state and interaction history evolve. WorldLines (Zhang et al., 2026d) pairs evidence-linked memory questions with embodied planning over semantic household traces; this protocol evaluates state maintenance without establishing raw visual or acoustic retention. WorldMemArena (Liu et al., 2026c) evaluates memory formation, maintenance, retrieval, and use across multi-session action–world interaction. RoboMME-Interference (Rathi, 2026) measures retrieval robustness as unrelated prior sessions accumulate. WorldLines and WorldMemArena therefore extend evaluation from access to T1 Static Memory toward maintenance and revision under T2 Dynamic Memory, whereas RoboMME-Interference isolates interference during access. Most current benchmarks nevertheless rely on simulated or hybrid environments, and few systematically test conflicting memories (CF), unanswerable queries (UQ), lifelong updating in physical environments, or failure attribution across memory-lifecycle stages.

7.3 Application Regimes

Application regimes are distinguished here by the function memory serves rather than by input modality. They consolidate concrete downstream tasks—including multimodal recall, long-form video and audio understanding, personalized interaction, GUI automation, embodied control, and iterative generation—according to the role memory plays in the resulting system. This view is orthogonal to Axis I: the same images, audio, documents, or interaction traces may be retained to support evidence-based decisions, continuity with a user, execution in an environment, or consistency in generated content. Each regime consequently stresses a different property of memory.

7.3.1 Recall and Evidence-Based Reasoning

This regime encompasses multimodal question answering, episodic retrieval, and long-form video or audio understanding. Although these tasks operate over different evidence—from visual details and temporally distributed events to speakers and acoustic cues—they share the requirement that later outputs remain grounded in recoverable observations (Jiang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025a; Someki et al., 2026). Personal archives and long-document assistants require cross-modal retrieval and source grounding, whereas enterprise analysis additionally requires evidence to remain attributable across files, reporting periods, and tool outputs. MARDoc, for example, distils long-document interaction traces into structured evidence and reasoning memories and checks whether the recovered evidence is sufficient (Chen et al., 2026b). Financial reasoning makes the temporal and numerical demands especially explicit: FinAcumen selectively reuses successful strategies and failure-derived cautions while coordinating retrieval, visual decoding, calculation, and verification over text, tables, charts, and time-indexed records (Guo et al., 2026d). The central memory property is therefore not recall volume alone, but recoverable provenance and temporal validity, since persistence without these safeguards can retain stale or weakly grounded evidence.

7.3.2 Personalization and Cross-Session Continuity

Personalization uses memory to maintain a user-specific state across otherwise disconnected encounters. Relevant experience may include stated preferences, prior dialogue, viewed media, corrections, and recurring activity patterns. M2A combines complementary memory layers for long-term multimodal interaction, TAME maintains a state-aware personalized context without additional training, and Persode grounds a visual-journaling assistant in episodic personal history (Feng et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2025a). In consumer settings, the resulting continuity supports recommendations and assistance; analogous requirements arise in enterprise workflows that carry user, team, or account context across sessions. More recently, LLM-based individual simulation has attracted growing interest. The pioneering Individual Turing Test highlights the value of memory in capturing personal opinions and preferences (Guo et al., 2026c), which could be more faithful through multimodal personal histories beyond text. This regime stresses identity scoping, selective retention, and revision: useful continuity requires the agent to associate evidence with the correct subject and to update preferences without allowing obsolete or cross-user information to persist.

7.3.3 Control and Task Execution

Control applications require memory to change what an agent does, not merely what it can report. They include GUI workflow automation, spatial navigation and mapping, embodied manipulation and planning, and the transfer of procedures learned from demonstrations or prior experience (Wen et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2022; Mandlekar et al., 2023; Garrett et al., 2025; Hsu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026f). MAGNET, for instance, evolves visual-semantic and procedural memories so that GUI skills transfer across changing interfaces (Sun et al., 2026d). In embodied settings, remembered layouts, object states, and task progress support navigation and manipulation under partial observability, while environment states and action outcomes provide direct evidence of memory utility (Yadav et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026c; Bjorck et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2025). The same principle extends to other domains. FinAgent combines numerical, textual, and visual market evidence with diversified memory retrieval and dual-level reflection to adapt its decisions as market conditions change (Zhang et al., 2024). Enterprise automation adds operational constraints and heterogeneous artifacts: Matrix refines experience-derived memory to specialize agents for recurring business-document extraction, while MemoPhishAgent retrieves episodic reasoning trajectories to orchestrate tools for recurring and novel phishing threats (Liu et al., 2026f; Chen et al., 2026g). The defining property is action relevance under change: stored experience must improve the present decision while remaining revisable when interfaces, environments, document formats, market conditions, or threat patterns evolve.

7.3.4 Generation and World Consistency

Generative applications use memory to preserve constraints, entities, style, and causal state across iterative production. Unlike recall and control, however, this regime remains weakly represented by dedicated memory benchmarks: existing generation tasks commonly evaluate open-ended responses rather than image, video, or speech synthesis with persistent identity and world state. Application systems nevertheless demonstrate the underlying demand. MemSlides separates profile, working, and tool memories to support personalized slide creation and local revision, while agentic video systems retain executable event structures to keep generated scenes aligned with an evolving plan (Jin et al., 2026c; Cudlenco et al., 2026). Financial reporting combines this consistency requirement with evidence grounding. FinSight’s variable memory unifies financial data, tools, and intermediate analyses before synthesizing citation-aware narratives, tables, and charts (Jin et al., 2026a). Here memory is valuable because generation is not a single decoding pass: evidence is collected, transformed, assessed, visualized, and revised over multiple stages. The regime therefore stresses versioned state and recoverable dependencies, so that a change to an underlying fact or analytical result can propagate coherently through the final multimodal artifact.

7.4 Application–Evaluation Alignment and Gaps

The benchmark landscape is broader in modality than in lifecycle coverage. This pattern is partly determined by the downstream tasks used for evaluation. Image, video, and audio benchmarks predominantly use question answering, retrieval, or localization, which expose recall and grounding but provide limited evidence of subsequent memory use. GUI and embodied benchmarks instead evaluate action or planning through interface states, environment transitions, and task success (Liu et al., 2026d; Yadav et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026c). The task therefore determines which aspects of memory can be observed, whereas the capability dimensions characterize the memory demands being evaluated.

This task dependence leads to uneven coverage across the application regimes in Section 7.3. Long-range and cross-modal evidence access supports many important applications and, correspondingly, constitutes the dominant evaluation target across Table 2. State tracking is increasingly considered in personalized, interactive, and embodied settings. Conflict resolution and evidence insufficiency remain sparsely evaluated, however, and memory-grounded action is concentrated in GUI and embodied benchmarks. Consequently, retrieval-centric applications are better represented in current benchmarks than applications that require persistent state maintenance, conflict handling, or memory-grounded action. Current evaluation therefore establishes whether experience can be recovered more consistently than whether it remains valid, sufficient, and actionable.

Modality-specific evaluation is strongest for structure native to each input stream. Image benchmarks emphasize visual details, entities, and state changes (Jiang et al., 2025b; Ren et al., 2026); video benchmarks emphasize temporal localization and multi-event reasoning (Yang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026e); audio and speech benchmarks examine long-form retrieval, speaker- and acoustic-level retention, and stateful interaction (Someki et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2025b). GUI and embodied benchmarks instead focus on interface, spatial, object, and task states (Yadav et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026c). Audio evaluation nevertheless remains predominantly recall- or transcription-oriented, with limited coverage of persistent correction, personalized response, speaker conflict, abstention, and memory-grounded action.

Lifecycle coverage remains concentrated on persistence and retrieval in T1 Static Memory; state-update and experience-reuse tasks probe T2 Dynamic Memory, but usually under stable policies. A Learn label therefore does not establish T3 Self-Evolving Memory unless deployment feedback produces persistent changes to a reusable memory-management policy (Zeng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026e). Thus, although current benchmarks cover important application-facing retrieval capabilities, their lifecycle coverage remains incomplete. The main gaps lie in conflict and uncertainty handling, source provenance, end-to-end memory attribution, policy adaptation, and memory-grounded visual generation.

8 Challenges and Outlook

The preceding sections show that long-term multimodal agent memory depends on three coupled concerns: what experience is retained and how it is represented, how that memory is maintained as new evidence arrives, and how its logical operations are realized under finite system resources. Their interaction becomes more consequential over long trajectories, changing environments, and shared deployments. We therefore distinguish challenges in formation and representation, challenges in memory management, and tensions between the two, followed by deployment-oriented evaluation and open infrastructure problems. The infrastructure discussion builds on Section 6 and focuses on how the assumptions and guarantees of the analyzed mechanisms can be integrated under sustained deployment.

8.1 Multimodal Memory Formation and Representation

Memory formation determines not only what information is retained, but also what can still be recovered after the original experience has been transformed, what can later be located and changed inside the resulting representation, and how far any of this has been worked out beyond the modalities that dominate current practice. Current systems use a wide range of source, explicit, latent, and parametric representations, yet important questions remain about what each of them should preserve, what structure each should expose, and whether the answers established for visual experience carry over to other modalities.

8.1.1 Recovering Supporting Evidence

Abstraction should move from lossy compression toward recoverable representation. As previous sections show, modality-specific encodings, textual, structured, latent, and parametric memories can all remove information that remains available in source-level evidence. Source-linked designs introduced in Section 3.4 partly address this problem by preserving links from derived memories back to supporting observations. The remaining question is what information should be preserved during formation so that this recoverability is reliable.

Existing systems use different combinations of timestamps (Wang et al., 2025a), source identifiers (Feng et al., 2026), entity links (Long et al., 2026), spatial references (Liu et al., 2025b), and pointers to supporting observations (Lin et al., 2026d). However, a substantial portion of the analyzed architectures do not retain a usable route back to the evidence from which their memories were formed. Among those that do, the route is often simply that the source was never abstracted away, rather than a link deliberately carried by a derived memory, and where such links do exist they differ in what they record. Provenance is therefore seldom a designed property of the representation. A useful direction is to define a minimal provenance bundle for formed memories, containing enough information to identify where a memory came from, how it was produced, and what evidence supports it. The required fields may differ across modalities and representation types, but provenance should be treated as part of the representation itself rather than as optional metadata.

Recoverable representation does not require every source observation to be retained indefinitely. Instead, memory formation should make explicit which information may be discarded and which supporting evidence must remain reachable for later inspection or reinterpretation. This would make abstraction more controlled without requiring all downstream memories to preserve the full original experience. What remains open is how to make this decision. Current systems use different rules (Shen et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a), but a better criterion should balance retention cost against the need to verify or correct information later.

8.1.2 Finding and Updating Specific Memory

Formed memory should expose the units that memory management acts on. While recoverability asks whether a memory can be traced back to its supporting evidence, semantic addressability asks whether specific content can be identified and changed within the representation itself. Explicit textual and structured records provide such units by construction, which is why they support revision and conflict resolution most directly (Bo et al., 2026). Semantic addressability remains rare outside these representations. The difficulty is sharpest in latent and parametric memory, which is compact and integrates directly with the model’s computation but does not expose content as separately identifiable units by construction. An update to such memory may therefore reach information it was not intended to change, and the system may not be able to identify which part of memory is responsible for a particular behaviour.

This limitation appears in the corpus as a pattern rather than only as an argument. Section 5.4 shows that every architecture evolving a memory-management policy at deployment time maintains an explicit cross-represented component, and that none whose memory is only latent or only parametric does so. The absence is not a matter of these systems being static: most latent-only architectures do update their memory state under a fixed policy. What they lack is not dynamism, but clearly identifiable units over which memory-management decisions can be attributed, inspected, and revised. Source-preserving memory shows the same absence despite being addressable in another sense, and the contrast is instructive: its units can be identified perceptually, by time or position, yet still not at the semantic level at which a write or retention decision is made. The obstacle is therefore not distributed representation as such, but the absence of units that correspond to what a policy decides about.

Parametric memory can already be divided into separable modules associated with different experiences, modalities, or tasks, as in adapter banks that hold per-task procedures (Si et al., 2026), per-video parameters (Suri et al., 2026), or modality-specific edits (Seong et al., 2025). This makes parts of a distributed representation easier to locate and manipulate, but it has not so far produced semantic addressability: among the analyzed systems that organize memory this way, the few that evolve a management policy during deployment do so through an explicit cross-represented component rather than through the parameter store itself. Structured latent memory that binds persistent state to identifiable slots or entities (Chung et al., 2026) would be a further step in the same direction. What a fuller answer requires is nonetheless clear: a distributed memory is addressable in the sense that management needs only when the same unit can be identified, revised on its own, and afterwards verified to have changed while the rest of memory did not. The open question is whether that combination can be achieved without losing the compactness and direct model integration that motivate latent and parametric memory in the first place.

8.2 Multimodal Memory Management

Section 4 describes how memory changes after formation, from fixed retrieval to persistent maintenance and feedback-driven policy evolution. The challenges collected here concern two questions that arise once memory is allowed to change over time: how the system should keep its memory up to date as new experience arrives, and how the policies that manage memory can themselves improve from feedback.

8.2.1 Maintaining Up-to-Date Memory

Memory maintenance should move from recording change toward keeping track of which state is still valid. New observations can be appended, existing memories can be revised, and repeated evidence can be merged, but these operations do not by themselves tell the system whether an older state still holds, has been replaced, or should be kept only as history. This becomes especially important in multimodal settings, where evidence about the same object, event, or user may arrive at different times and through different modalities. The difficulty here concerns observations of the same state that arrive separately, not disagreement among the stored representations derived from them.

A timestamp records when an observation was made, not how long what it asserts remains true. In multimodal settings the two can come apart in a particular way. A visual observation may show where an object was seen, while a later instruction may report that it has moved. A new image may correct an earlier description, while the older observation remains useful as historical evidence. Where staleness is handled at all, it is often handled by removing or replacing the outdated record (Yeo et al., 2026b), or by checking a cached state against a fresh observation at the moment of use (Liu et al., 2025c), rather than by representing how long a belief remains valid.

A promising direction is to explicitly model this status within the memory management process. A memory may be marked as current, historical, superseded, uncertain, or still valid alongside another state. Such decisions may depend on the source and reliability of new evidence rather than on recency alone. They may also need to distinguish when an observation is received from when the event it describes actually happened. What remains open is how an agent should decide when new evidence replaces an older state, when both should coexist, and when uncertainty should be preserved rather than resolved.

8.2.2 Self-Improving Memory Management

Keeping memory up to date assumes that the rules for doing so are already good enough. The next challenge is to improve those rules from experience. As Section 4.3 describes, feedback-driven memory management changes how memories are written, maintained, or retrieved during deployment. This is different from optimizing a controller during training and then freezing it: once deployment begins, a frozen controller continues to apply a stable policy even as the memory contents change.

Current policy evolution is concentrated on retrieval, while changes to write and maintenance policies remain much less common. One likely reason is that retrieval receives relatively direct feedback: the system can often observe whether retrieved memory helped the next answer or action. The effect of an earlier write, merge, revision, or forgetting decision may appear much later, and in a multimodal agent it may not appear in the same modality at all. A memory written from a visual observation may be revealed as wrong only by a later instruction, by an observation in another modality, or by the failure of an action taken on its basis. Credit therefore has to travel across both time and modality before it can reach the decision that should change.

A useful direction is to connect later success and failure back to the memory decision that most likely caused it. This would allow feedback-driven improvement to extend beyond retrieval without treating every downstream error as evidence that the entire memory policy should change. What remains open is how to assign delayed and cross-modal feedback to earlier memory decisions while separating their effects from the many other operations that occur in between.

8.3 Representation–Management Tensions in Multimodal Memory

Section 5 shows that representation and memory management cannot be designed independently. What a memory preserves limits what later operations can inspect, change, verify, or remove. At the same time, the way memory is managed determines which parts of a representation remain useful over long interactions. The challenges here arise from this coupling. They are not problems of representation or management alone, but cases in which one limits what the other can do.

8.3.1 Editable Representations without Loss of Detail

Multimodal memory should preserve perceptual detail without making later correction difficult. Source observations and modality-specific representations retain information that may disappear after an image, video, trajectory, or other observation is converted into text or structure. Yet the same abstraction that loses detail often makes memory easier to revise. A textual fact or graph entry can be changed directly, while correcting one semantic detail inside a long video, a distributed latent state, or a parameter update is much less straightforward. What a representation preserves therefore limits how precisely memory can later be maintained, both in how narrowly an update can be scoped and in how directly its result can be checked.

Hybrid and source-linked designs reduce this tension by keeping an abstract memory together with a route back to supporting evidence (Wang et al., 2026e; Fan et al., 2026a). But coexistence alone does not settle the problem. An abstract record can become outdated while the source observation remains valid as historical evidence. A new observation may also contradict the current abstraction without making the older evidence useless. The system must then decide which layer should guide current behavior and when the source should be reopened rather than trusting the abstraction.

A useful direction is to combine editable memory state with recoverable modality-specific evidence and an explicit rule for moving between them. Routine updates can operate on compact textual or structured state, while uncertain or high-impact changes can return to the supporting image, video, audio segment, or trajectory for verification. What remains open is how much source detail must stay reachable for later correction without making long-term memory expensive to maintain.

8.3.2 Selective Evidence Retention for Verifiable Memory

Verifiable memory should not require every past observation to remain available forever. Retained source evidence, provenance, version history, and checkpoints make memory changes easier to inspect and reverse. In multimodal memory, however, the cost of keeping this support depends strongly on what form the evidence takes. A short textual record, selected image frames, a long video, an audio segment, a 3D trajectory, and a latent or parametric checkpoint impose very different storage and processing costs. The representation therefore limits how much evidence a management system can realistically keep for later verification.

Current systems usually make this choice implicitly through what their memory architecture happens to retain, rather than through an explicit policy for verification. Some retain source observations (Wang et al., 2026j), some retain only derived records (Gao et al., 2025), and others keep checkpoints or structured state (Gu et al., 2024). What is often missing is a rule for which evidence deserves long-term retention, which evidence can be compressed, and which updates are important enough to justify preserving an earlier version.

A useful direction is selective verification. Lightweight provenance can remain available for most memories, while expensive source evidence or checkpoints are kept only when later inspection is likely to matter. High-impact revisions, uncertain memories, or information supported by conflicting modalities may justify stronger evidence retention than routine observations. The open problem is how to predict this need before the future correction or dispute actually occurs. A system that keeps too little loses the ability to verify its memory, while one that keeps everything gives up much of the benefit of abstraction.

8.3.3 Policy Adaptation with Preserved Evidence Grounding

Self-improving memory management should not silently change what evidence the agent relies on. As Section 4.3 describes, a policy may evolve how memory is written, maintained, or retrieved. In a multimodal system, such a change can also alter the path through which information reaches the agent. A retrieval policy may gradually favor textual summaries over visual evidence, a write policy may compress one modality more aggressively, or a maintenance policy may preserve some forms of memory while discarding others. Management evolution can therefore change not only performance, but also which representations continue to support that performance.

This creates a stability problem that task accuracy alone may not reveal. A revised policy can maintain or even improve short-term answers while relying less on the modality that originally grounded them. For example, a system may answer correctly from a cached textual summary while rarely reopening the visual evidence from which that summary was formed. If the summary later becomes wrong, the loss of that evidence path may only become visible much later. Current policy-evolution methods rarely evaluate whether adaptation changes the balance of evidence used across representations.

A useful direction is to evaluate policy changes together with the evidence paths they alter. Before a new policy is accepted, the system should check not only whether downstream performance improves, but also whether access to supporting modalities and representations has been weakened. This may require tracking which memory paths support important decisions and comparing that use before and after adaptation. What remains open is how much change in evidence use is healthy adaptation and when it becomes a loss of grounding that should block or reverse the policy update.

8.3.4 Sustaining Memory without Losing the Ability to Forget

Long-term memory should remain bounded without losing control over what can be removed. The difficulty depends on representation. Retained images, videos, audio, and trajectories grow with experience; structured memory grows with entities, events, and relations; a bank of adapters can grow with tasks or episodes; and a fixed-size latent state faces a different problem, because new information must compete with what is already encoded. Representation therefore determines what grows, while memory management determines how that growth can be contained.

Existing systems use operations such as consolidation (Rasheed and Kabtoul, 2026), compression (Li et al., 2026a), eviction (Lin et al., 2026c), decay (Sun et al., 2026b), and forgetting (Liu et al., 2025a), but sustained memory growth under a fixed budget remains weakly addressed. A useful direction is representation-aware budgeting. The system should not apply one retention rule to every memory form. Source evidence may be sampled or compressed, structured records may be merged, latent capacity may need to be reallocated, and parametric modules may need consolidation or removal. The hard part is deciding what can be reduced without destroying information whose value will only become clear later.

Capacity is only one reason to remove memory. Some information may need to disappear because it is outdated, corrected, or explicitly deleted. In a multimodal system, that information may already have spread from a source observation into a caption, embedding, graph node, summary, latent state, or parameter update. Removing one copy therefore does not establish that the information is gone. This also creates a direct tension with Section 8.3.2: verification benefits from retaining evidence and version history, while deletion may require the same evidence and history to disappear.

A useful direction is to specify forgetting as a cross-representation outcome rather than as the removal of a single record. Provenance and derivation links can identify the captions, embeddings, structured entries, summaries, or parameter modules that may carry the targeted information, but locating a derivative does not guarantee that the information can be selectively erased from it. The memory policy must determine which information should become unavailable, which unrelated knowledge should remain, and how the outcome can be verified. This also makes the tension with reversibility explicit: retaining an earlier version may support correction but conflict with a removal requirement. The open representational problem is especially difficult for latent states and shared parameters, where the targeted information is not separately addressable. Section 6.6 examines relevant coordination mechanisms, while Section 8.5 addresses how a declared removal reaches replicas and active derivatives and when that operation can be considered complete.

8.4 Deployment-Oriented Memory Evaluation

Evaluation determines which forms of progress become visible. Current benchmarks establish increasingly broad coverage across modalities and tasks, yet long-term memory is ultimately valuable as a process that preserves, updates, accesses, and applies experience under continuing interaction. Future evaluation should expose this process, stress it over sustained horizons and bounded resources, and test it under the operating conditions faced by deployed agents.

8.4.1 Lifecycle-Aware Evaluation

Multimodal memory evaluation should move from outcome-level scoring toward stage-resolved diagnosis. Many existing benchmarks summarize performance with final answer accuracy or task success, including long-video reasoning and interactive visual-recall settings (Long et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026c). These scores establish whether the complete system succeeded, while leaving the origin of failure unresolved. Recent benchmarks demonstrate the value of richer supervision through evidence annotations, update points, retrieval judgments, feedback-reuse tests, and memory-specific execution metrics (Liu et al., 2026c; Liu et al., 2026e; Chai et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026d). A lifecycle-aware protocol can organize such signals around four observable stages.

Formation.

Evaluation should determine whether the agent identifies the parts of an experience that will matter later and forms faithful memory from them. Useful process metrics include coverage of gold memory points, correctness and supportedness of written records, rates of hallucinated or irrelevant entries, preservation of source links, and retention of task-relevant visual, acoustic, spatial, and temporal detail. These signals evaluate selective writing and representation quality before later retrieval can conceal their failures.

Maintenance.

Evaluation should track whether persistent memory remains valid as new evidence arrives. Intermediate metrics can measure successful incorporation of current state, rejection or supersession of stale records, conflict resolution, faithfulness of consolidation, and consistency across source, textual, structured, latent, or parametric representations. Versioned memory snapshots and annotated state transitions can further reveal when an initially correct memory becomes corrupted during update, compression, or reorganization.

Access.

Evaluation should assess whether the evidence required by the current decision is recovered from the appropriate memory path. Evidence recall, precision, ranking quality, temporal or spatial localization, cross-modal coverage, and retrieval latency expose distinct access failures. Comparing ordinary retrieval with oracle evidence also separates limitations of memory access from those of the downstream reasoner.

Utilization.

Evaluation should verify that accessed memory actually guides the response, plan, or action. Evidence-conditioned correctness, source attribution, adherence to the current state under conflict, action–outcome consistency, and recovery after feedback provide process-level measures of memory use. Counterfactual removal or replacement of retrieved evidence can further test whether an apparently correct output causally depends on memory. For generative agents, utilization should additionally test whether retrieved constraints preserve entity, style, temporal state, and world consistency, and whether subsequent memory updates propagate coherently through later revisions of the generated artifact.

Few benchmarks expose all four stages, and complete lifecycle supervision is especially scarce for native multimodal evidence. Establishing shared trajectory annotations and stage-level metrics would make memory failures localizable, allow process rewards to target the operation that failed, and support meaningful comparison among architectures whose final accuracy may be similar for very different reasons.

8.4.2 Long-Horizon and Resource-Aware Evaluation

Long-horizon evaluation should measure sustained memory quality under the resource pressure created by accumulating multimodal experience. The field has begun to extend temporal scale: M3-Bench evaluates videos averaging roughly half an hour (Long et al., 2026), StreamArena reaches hour-scale causal streams (Zhang et al., 2026c), EgoLife records a week of shared daily experience (Yang et al., 2025a), and EgoMonth spans 20–120 days of egocentric observations (Chen et al., 2026f). This progression brings evaluation closer to the timescale of persistent assistants. Continuous deployment protocols with interleaved writing, maintenance, querying, and feedback remain much less developed; even long multi-session histories are often frozen and queried offline (Ren et al., 2026).

Resource pressure.

As the observation stream grows, a memory system consumes persistent storage, write-time computation, retrieval bandwidth, model context, and response time. Evaluation should therefore impose explicit budgets and report memory size and growth rate, ingestion throughput and lag, retrieval latency, token or compute cost per unit of experience, and the fraction of source evidence retained at each fidelity level. Early studies already expose large differences in write–read latency and execution cost across memory designs (Liu et al., 2026c; Liu et al., 2026d); standardized budgets would turn these isolated measurements into comparable operating constraints. Systems accounting should also distinguish the size of logical memory from the total physical footprint of its replicas, indices, cached execution states, and temporary buffers. In addition to end-to-end latency and memory quality, experiments should report peak accelerator occupancy, transferred bytes, and the costs of materialization, decompression, and recomputation. Warm-cache and cold-cache conditions should be identified separately, and construction or background write-back should not be treated as free when their costs are shifted outside the query interval. These measurements connect the quality–resource frontier to the mechanisms in Section 6 without reducing memory quality to cache hit rate.

Longitudinal degradation.

A bounded memory must continually decide what to preserve, consolidate, or forget. Its evaluation should trace accuracy, evidence recall, update correctness, grounding, and action quality as a function of elapsed time, accumulated experience, and available memory. Context-length analyses and time-stratified forgetting curves provide useful starting points (Ren et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026b), while deployment-oriented protocols should also reveal delayed corruption, retrieval slowdown, representation drift, and the compounding effect of early writing errors on later decisions. The central comparison is the quality–resource frontier: how reliably a system preserves useful, verifiable memory as its operating horizon grows under a fixed budget.

8.4.3 Real-World Deployment

Deployment evaluation should reproduce the conditions under which multimodal memory must operate continuously. Real environments combine strict response deadlines, imperfect sensing, asynchronous feedback, open-ended tasks, and changes in users and worlds. Benchmarks increasingly incorporate real egocentric recordings, interactive interfaces, and evolving state (Yang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2026f; Liu et al., 2026d; Liu et al., 2026c), while most still isolate these factors within curated data, controlled state transitions, or resettable environments.

Real-time operation.

An agent that recalls the correct evidence after the decision window has passed cannot provide effective assistance. Evaluation should measure end-to-end response latency, deadline-miss rate, proactive trigger timing, and the delay between observation and query-visible memory availability. RIVER couples memory accuracy with temporal distance and response timing, while StreamArena measures query-to-answer latency across routing, recall, external search, and inference (Shi et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026c). Extending these protocols to continuous memory writing and maintenance would expose whether background processing can keep pace with the incoming multimodal stream. For deployments requiring failure recovery, the time to a recoverable commit and behavior after interrupted writes should be measured separately under an explicit failure model; query visibility alone does not establish durability.

Perceptual and environmental robustness.

Deployment streams contain motion blur, occlusion, poor lighting, overlapping speech, sensor dropout, uncertain timestamps, and incomplete or contradictory feedback. Systems also encounter devices, interfaces, locations, speakers, and object appearances outside the distributions represented in curated benchmarks. Evaluation should introduce controlled corruptions alongside naturally noisy trajectories, vary which modalities remain available, and test whether memory preserves uncertainty, requests clarification, or abstains when the evidence is insufficient. Robustness should be measured across both memory formation and later reuse, since an unnoticed perceptual error can persist long after the original observation has disappeared.

Continual user and world change.

Long-running agents must follow changing preferences, identities, routines, goals, interface states, and physical environments. Evaluation should present irregular state changes, delayed corrections, cross-modal disagreement, and multiple users whose memories must remain separated. The resulting metrics should capture adaptation delay, stale-memory use, recovery after correction, cross-user contamination, and retention of valid historical evidence. Such protocols would connect benchmark success to the defining requirement of deployed memory: maintaining reliable continuity while the world that memory describes continues to change.

8.5 Memory Infrastructure and Efficiency

Section 6 examines mechanisms for residency, restoration, reuse, materialization, and coordination. The open systems problem is how their assumptions and guarantees can compose over the lifetime of changing multimodal memory under bounded resources. The directions below concern runtime decisions and guarantees. They complement the representational and management requirements in Section 8.3 and the evaluation protocols in Section 8.4.

8.5.1 Workflow-Responsive Residency and Data Movement

Program- and workflow-aware systems already exploit execution phase, relative idleness, and anticipated reuse (Kang et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026b; Pan et al., 2025). The next question is how placement and transfer execution should respond when those signals change while data is in flight. TokenCake, for example, already triggers an immediate upload when a tool returns earlier than predicted (Bian et al., 2027). A broader runtime contract should address branch cancellation, overlapping readers, and reprioritization across storage tiers: which transfers can be interrupted, which must drain, when staging buffers can be reused, and whether completed chunks remain useful. Research should connect transfer granularity and queue depth to bounded wasted traffic and resumption delay, rather than treating cancellation as an instantaneous reversal of offload.

Compression should also be optimized over repeated use rather than a single transfer. Building on the transport and compute–load mechanisms in Section 6.3, future designs should jointly account for encoding, decompression, temporary storage, layout conversion, and the number of expected restorations. Incremental restoration may reduce startup delay, but finer transfer units add metadata and scheduling overhead. Quality analysis should distinguish repeatedly decoding one unchanged compressed artifact from repeatedly re-encoding or approximately reconstructing its outputs; only the latter introduces an additional chain of potentially accumulating approximation. The objective is a lifetime cost–quality trade-off, not network-byte reduction alone.

8.5.2 Dependency-Aware Reuse and Scheduling

The dependency assumptions of prefix caching and selective recomputation in Section 6.4 become harder to track when memory is revised, reordered, cropped, or materialized through a different model interface. Future work should investigate compact dependency descriptions that connect execution artifacts to their source versions and relevant transformations, such as preprocessing, encoder or adapter versions, prompt composition, positions, and attention configuration. These descriptions should distinguish exact reuse from empirically validated approximation and permit selective invalidation or reconstruction. An unresolved trade-off is granularity: coarse dependencies cause unnecessary recomputation, while fine-grained tracking can cost more than the computation it saves.

Scheduling should use this information without collapsing relevance into cache locality. Preble establishes the value of balancing prefix reuse with worker load (Srivatsa et al., 2025); multimodal memory introduces additional choices among available evidence representations and materialization paths. Research should optimize worker selection, cache admission, prefetching, and reconstruction jointly, subject to the evidence, freshness, and quality requirements of the task. Reuse value must include validation overhead, expected remaining uses before invalidation, and interference with other programs. A high hit rate is not a sufficient objective when the hits are expensive to restore, likely to be invalidated before further use, or available only for evidence that is less appropriate to the current decision.

8.5.3 Coordinating Materialization and Write-back

Read-side acceleration can shift cost into memory construction rather than eliminate it. Existing workload characterization separates construction, retrieval, and generation costs, while FOLIO illustrates asynchronous construction with a recent-evidence path (Omri et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026a). Future systems should jointly schedule foreground inference and background encoding, summarization, indexing, or adapter production. The key decisions are when to materialize expensive artifacts, when to defer work until demand is known, and how to prevent persistent write backlogs from making new experience unavailable. These decisions should consider expected reuse and invalidation, not just instantaneous GPU utilization.

Such orchestration also needs representation-specific fallbacks. When a compact record is not ready, a runtime may expose retained source evidence; when a model-specific artifact is incompatible, it may reconstruct a compatible form from an authorized source. These alternatives are not semantically interchangeable and should operate within the memory policy’s requirements, rather than silently replacing evidence to meet a latency target. Research should determine when eager materialization, lazy reconstruction, or incremental publication provides the best balance of responsiveness, groundedness, and recoverability. Systems evaluation in Section 8.4 should account for the costs incurred on both sides of this read–write boundary.

8.5.4 Cross-Layer Consistency, Recovery, and Revocation

The scoped guarantees in Section 6.6 motivate explicit publication and recovery contracts across artifacts. Future work should specify whether a read requires a consistent snapshot, read-your-writes visibility, or bounded staleness, and how these requirements span source media, semantic records, retrieval indices, and derived execution state. The coordination granularity need not be the entire memory bank; a versioned set of dependent artifacts may be sufficient. The challenge is to expose a coherent read path while expensive derivatives are being rebuilt, without globally blocking unrelated requests.

Durability should be specified separately from logical retention and query visibility. For deployments that require recovery from failures, research should identify which source records, versions, and transformation results must be committed, which caches can be reconstructed, and how interrupted write-back can resume without duplicating or exposing incomplete records. Preserving source media alone may not reproduce a prior stochastic summary or parameter update. The required guarantee must therefore distinguish recovery of the exact previous artifact from reconstruction of a newly generated alternative.

Deletion and permission changes extend coordination to already materialized state. Whereas Section 8.3.4 asks what must be forgotten and how to verify that outcome, the infrastructure question is how a declared removal propagates through replicas, indices, summaries, contexts, caches, and retained versions. Future work should define a completion boundary and distinguish preventing new retrieval from retiring active derivatives and reclaiming storage. Collaborative Memory’s retrieval-time access control provides one boundary, not a demonstrated solution for all downstream artifacts (Rezazadeh et al., 2025). Dependency metadata can identify retirement targets, but cannot by itself establish semantic erasure from a distributed latent state or shared model parameters.

MemOS proposes common abstractions for heterogeneous memory resources, while MemoryOS organizes hierarchical memory for agent interaction (Li et al., 2025b; Kang et al., 2025). Building on such efforts, the objective should be interoperable contracts for identity, version, provenance, compatibility, and lifetime—not a universal representation that erases modality-specific semantics. The central open problem is to make their guarantees compose under finite resources and partial failure while preserving the evidence needed for future reasoning and correction.

9 Conclusion

The central question of multimodal agent memory is what evidence to retain from heterogeneous multimodal experience, how to represent it for subsequent reasoning and action, and how to keep it valid over time. Our framework characterizes multimodal agent memory along two axes: Formation and Representation, and Memory Management. Axis I classifies the operative representation through which retained experience becomes available to downstream computation; Axis II distinguishes T1 Static Memory, T2 Dynamic Memory and T3 Self-Evolving Memory. Joint analysis of the two axes shows that representation constrains the accessibility, revisability, verifiability, and recoverability of memory. The coexistence of multiple representations further requires maintaining provenance links, temporal validity, and cross-representation consistency, and updating memory state is not equivalent to evolving the management policy. Current systems remain dominated by fixed memory and memory updating through stable policies. Online policy evolution, bounded lifelong memory, governed forgetting, and lifecycle-aware evaluation remain underdeveloped. At the systems level, current infrastructure lacks unified mechanisms for efficiently and consistently storing, restoring, and reusing memory under finite resource constraints; while existing benchmarks remain insufficient to establish whether memories remain valid, sufficient, and actionable throughout the full memory lifecycle. Together, these challenges point toward a multimodal memory system for long-term operation that preserves verifiable and recoverable multimodal evidence under bounded resources, maintains temporally evolving and cross-representation-consistent memory states, and uses continual feedback to improve its memory-management policies.
